In this passage, gratitude is not merely a feeling that follows the blessing — it is bound up with the very sign that the blessing has come.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary here by noting that he will elaborate more on this subject at the beginning of Surah Maryam (chapter 19), Allah willing.

passages.title: The angels' address to Mary's chosen purity
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These three ayat record a moment when angels address Maryam directly. They tell her what Allah has done for her — chosen her, purified her, chosen her above the women of the nations — and then, in the very next ayah, tell her what she must do: be devout to her Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow. The passage then turns from Maryam toward the Prophet ﷺ himself (ayah 44): *you were not there.* You were not present when the pens were cast; you were not present when they disputed. This is news of the unseen, revealed to you.

So the unit holds together as a single arc: **honour granted (42) → honour answered with worship (43) → and the whole account offered as proof that the one reciting it is a Prophet (44).**

---

## Ayah 42: chosen, purified, chosen again

Ibn Kathir notes that the angels spoke to Maryam **by Allah's command** — this was not their own initiative but a message delivered on His behalf. And he lists precisely why she was chosen: **her service to Him, her modesty, her honour, her innocence, and her conviction**, and because of her virtue over the women of the world.

Notice that this is a description of a life, not of a lucky accident. Allah's choosing is real and free — He chooses whom He wills — and Ibn Kathir ties it here to what she actually was: a servant, modest, honourable, innocent, certain in faith.

The wording of the ayah also names the choosing twice. Allah **chose** her — and **chose her above the women of the nations**; Ibn Kathir glosses this second phrase as her virtue over the women of the world. And between the two, the ayah places **purification**.

---

## "Above the women of the nations" — how far does it reach?

This phrase has been discussed carefully, because other reports also praise other women, and a reader may wonder how they fit together. The two sources in front of us each take up the question in their own way.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** speaks to it directly: the words *"and has chosen you over women of all the worlds"* in ayah 42 refer to **all women in that period of time**. Therefore, Maʿārif says, the statement appearing in hadith that **Fatimah is the foremost among the women of Paradise** does not contradict this ayah. (The source conveys this teaching without naming a collection for it, so it is passed on here as the meaning conveyed, not attributed to any particular book.)

**Ibn Kathir** treats the ayah under a heading of his own: *"The Virtue of Maryam Over the Women of Her Time."* Under it he brings these narrations:

**At-Tirmidhi** recorded that ʿAli bin Abi Talib said: *"I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:* **'The best woman (in her time) was Maryam, daughter of ʿImran, and the best woman (of the Prophet's time) is Khadijah (his wife), daughter of Khuwaylid.'"** Ibn Kathir adds that **the Two Sahihs** recorded this hadith.

Read the wording closely and you see each woman paired with a time: Maryam, the best woman in her time; Khadijah, the best woman of the Prophet's time.

**Ibn Jarir** recorded that Abu Musa al-Ashʿari said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Many men achieved perfection, but among women, only Maryam the daughter of ʿImran and Asiah, the wife of Firʿawn, achieved perfection."** Ibn Kathir notes that **the Six, with the exception of Abu Dawud**, recorded it, and that **al-Bukhari's** wording reads: *"Many men reached the level of perfection, but no woman reached such a level except Asiah, the wife of Firʿawn, and Maryam, the daughter of ʿImran. The superiority of ʿA'ishah (his wife) to other women is like the superiority of Tharid* (a meat and bread dish) *to other meals."* Ibn Kathir mentions that he gathered the various chains of narration and wordings of this hadith in the story of ʿIsa, son of Maryam, in his book *Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah*.

Two names stand together in that narration: Maryam, and Asiah the wife of Firʿawn. Whatever else separated their lives, the hadith places them side by side among those who reached perfection.

---

## Ayah 43: the honour turns instantly into a command

The angels do not leave Maryam with a compliment. In ayah 43 they say: **"O Maryam! Be devout to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow down with those who bow."**

Ibn Kathir explains that the angels **commanded Maryam to increase acts of worship** — humbleness, submission, prostration, bowing, and so forth — *"so that she would acquire what Allah had decreed for her, as a test for her."* And he adds that this test **also earned her a higher grade in this life and the Hereafter**, for through it Allah demonstrated His might by creating a son inside her without male intervention.

This is the hinge of the passage. Being chosen is not a resting place; it is a summons to more worship, and that worship is what readies her for what Allah had decreed. In Ibn Kathir's reading the test and the elevation are the same event seen from two sides.

**The word *qunut*.** The command *iqnutī* comes from *qunūt*. Ibn Kathir defines it plainly: **it means to submit with humbleness**. It is not merely carrying out an order; it is submission with lowliness before the One obeyed. He points to Allah's words elsewhere to fix the sense: *"Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth, and all surrender with obedience (**Qanitun**) to Him"* (al-Baqarah 2:116).

Note also the order the ayah gives: **be devout → prostrate → bow.**

**"With those who bow" — a lesson in how we bow.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to read past. The order to bow is qualified — *"bow down **with those who bow**"* — while no such qualification appears with the order to prostrate.

This, Maʿārif says, apparently seems to hint that **people generally do not observe due concern while making *rukūʿ*** (bowing). They tend to bend a little, then resume the standing position, as if in a hurry — a *rukūʿ* that is closer to standing (*qiyām*). So, Maʿārif continues, by mentioning the qualification *"those who bow"*, Allah Almighty has given **a model to be followed**, so that one's bowing in prayer could become similar to those who bow fully and perfectly, as is due.

**Living it:** the next time you go into *rukūʿ*, take it seriously — settle into it, let the back actually bow, do not treat it as the hurried gap between standing and prostrating. Maʿārif's reading of this one qualifying phrase quietly measures our *rukūʿ* against those who do it properly.

---

## Ayah 44: "You were not there"

Here the address shifts from Maryam to the Prophet ﷺ: **"This is a part of the news of the Ghayb (Unseen) which We reveal to you. You were not with them, when they cast lots with their pens as to which of them should be charged with the care of Maryam; nor were you with them when they disputed."**

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: *"You were not present, O Muhammad, when this occurred, so you cannot narrate what happened to the people as an eyewitness. Rather, Allah disclosed these facts to you as if you were a witness"* — when they conducted a lottery to choose the custodian of Maryam, **seeking the reward of this good deed**.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** states what the ayah is doing argumentatively: this verse **presents an argument to prove the prophethood of Sayyidna Muhammad ﷺ**, by referring to happenings in the lives of Sayyidna Zakariyya (peace be upon him) and Sayyidah Maryam. These took place in the remote past, with no likelihood of their being seen or heard or read — especially by him ﷺ — which by itself proves that his being so informed of the unknown was **beyond the ordinary course of learning**. He had no way of finding out such details by any obvious means at his command. Hence, Maʿārif concludes, this information was revealed to him as part of the message he gave to others.

And Maʿārif notes how precisely the ayah puts it: he ﷺ was not there to see them drawing lots by throwing their reed pens in water — on a prior agreement that **the owner of the pen which flows against the current shall be the winner** — nor was he present on the scene earlier, when they were **quarrelling** about the custody of Maryam before agreeing upon the drawing of lots. The ayah names both scenes.

---

## The story behind the pens

Ibn Kathir preserves the scene. **Ibn Jarir** recorded that **ʿIkrimah** said:

Maryam's mother left with Maryam, carrying her in her infant cloth, and took her to the rabbis from the offspring of Aaron, the brother of Musa. They were responsible for taking care of **Bayt al-Maqdis** (the Masjid) at that time, just as there were those who took care of the Kaʿbah. Maryam's mother said to them: *"Take this child whom I vowed [to serve the Masjid]. I have set her free, since she is my daughter, for no menstruating woman should enter the Masjid, and I shall not take her back home."*

They said: *"She is the daughter of our Imam"* — for ʿImran used to lead them in prayer and took care of their sacrificial rituals. **Zakariyya** said: *"Give her to me, for her maternal aunt is my wife."* They said: *"Our hearts cannot bear that you take her, for she is the daughter of our Imam."* So they conducted a lottery **with the pens with which they wrote the Tawrah**, and Zakariyya won the lottery and took Maryam into his care.

**ʿIkrimah, As-Suddi, Qatadah, ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas** and several others said that the rabbis went into the **Jordan river** and conducted a lottery there, deciding to throw their pens into the river: the pen that remained afloat and idle would indicate that its owner would take care of Maryam. When they threw their pens in, the water took all the pens under **except Zakariyya's pen, which remained afloat in its place.**

Ibn Kathir adds that Zakariyya was also **their master, chief, scholar, Imam and Prophet** — may Allah's peace and blessings be on him and the rest of the Prophets.

Read this alongside ayah 44 and the character of the dispute becomes clear: they were not arguing over who would be burdened with an orphan girl. As Ibn Kathir puts it, they conducted the lottery *seeking the reward of this good deed* — and Allah settled it in a way no one could contest.

---

## A ruling that grows out of the story: drawing lots (*qurʿah*)

Because the ayah mentions lots, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses to state the ruling, citing *Bayan al-Qur'an*, according to **the Hanafi jurists**:

- **Not permitted:** *qurʿah* cannot be given a decisive role in determining rights **already known and fixed in Islamic Law**. Drawing lots in such a situation is included under **qimar (gambling)**. Two examples are given: something jointly owned by several persons, where a lot is drawn so that the one whose name comes out takes **the whole thing**; and a child whose parentage is disputed, where a lot is drawn and whoever's name comes out is taken to be the father. Drawing lots in such cases is not allowed in the Shariʿah.

- **Permitted:** as for rights which **depend upon opinion**, *qurʿah* is permissible in them — for instance, while allotting portions of a joint property, A is given the eastern portion and B the western by drawing a lot. This is permissible **because it was permissible even without drawing lots**, by mutual agreement of the parties concerned or by a decree of a judge.

Maʿārif sums the principle up: **where the rights of all parties are equal, and the purpose of the lot is only to allocate equal portions and decide which portion is for whom, then drawing a lot is permissible.** The lot assigns what is already fairly owed — it does not create or destroy a right.

---

## What the passage asks of us

- **Honour from Allah is a call to work, not a place to sit.** The moment Maryam is told she is chosen, she is told to be devout, prostrate, and bow. If Allah has given you something — knowledge, protection, a place near His house, a good name — ayah 43 tells you what to do with it.
- **Worship is preparation.** Ibn Kathir reads her increased worship as what readied her for what Allah had decreed. The devotion built now is what will carry what comes later.
- **Give *rukūʿ* its due**, in the manner of "those who bow" — Maʿārif's quiet correction of a very common hurry.
- **Compete for service, not for status.** The custodians of Bayt al-Maqdis disputed over who would get to raise a child, *seeking the reward of this good deed*, as Ibn Kathir puts it.
- **The Qur'an's account of the unseen is itself evidence.** Ayah 44 invites the listener to ask a simple question — *how could he ﷺ know this?* — and Maʿārif answers it: this was beyond the ordinary course of learning, so it was revealed to him as part of the message he gave to others.

passages.title: The annunciation and mission of Jesus
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These seven ayat are one continuous piece of news. The angels announce to Maryam that she will bear a son — and in the same breath Allah tells her, in advance, who that son will be and what he will do: his names, his honour, his voice, his education, his miracles, his mission, and the single sentence he came to say. Nothing here is a separate topic. The announcement runs straight through to ayah 51, where 'Īsā (peace be upon him) speaks in his own voice: **"Truly, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him (Alone). This is the straight path."** Everything before it — the honour, the wonders, the Scripture — arrives at that line.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the flow: the previous verse, ayah 44, stood parenthetically between these verses and ayat 42–43, and its purpose was to affirm the prophethood of Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ. With ayah 45 the account of Sayyidah Maryam resumes, and it is preparing the ground for a fuller account of the birth, mission and miracles of Sayyidnā 'Īsā (peace be upon him).

---

## The announcement and what is packed into it (45–46)

**"(Remember) when the angels said: 'O Maryam! Verily, Allah gives you the glad tidings of a Word from Him, his name will be Al-Masīh, 'Īsā, the son of Maryam, held in honour in this world and in the Hereafter, and he will be one of those who are near to Allah. He will speak to the people, in the cradle and in manhood, and he will be one of the righteous.'"**

Ibn Kathir says simply that this ayah contains the glad tidings the angels brought to Maryam that she would give birth to a mighty son who will have a great future. Notice how much is folded into so few words.

**"A Word from Him."** Ibn Kathir explains this as *a son who will come into existence with a word from Allah, "Be," and he was.* He adds that this is also the meaning of what was said earlier concerning Yahyā — *"Believing in the Word from Allah"* (3:39) — and this, he says, is the position of the majority of the scholars.

**"Al-Masīh."** Ibn Kathir gives the derivation: he was called Al-Masīh, the Messiah, because when he *touched* (in Arabic, *Mash*) those afflicted with an illness, they would be healed **by Allah's leave**. Even inside the name, the qualifier is already there.

**"'Īsā, the son of Maryam."** This, Ibn Kathir says, is the name by which he will be known in this life, especially by the believers — and the phrase relates 'Īsā to his mother *because he did not have a father*.

**"Held in honour in this world and in the Hereafter, and one of those near to Allah."** Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves. In this world: he will be a leader, honoured by Allah because of the Law that Allah will reveal to him, the Scripture sent down to him, and the other bounties Allah will grant him. In the Hereafter: he will intercede with Allah, **by His leave**, on behalf of some people — just as is the case, Ibn Kathir says, with his brethren the mighty Messengers of Allah, peace be upon them all.

**Speaking in the cradle.** Ibn Kathir explains what the infant speech was *for*: calling to the worship of Allah alone without partners, while still in the cradle, as a miracle from Allah — and when he is a man, by Allah's revelation to him. The content is the same at both ends of his life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene: soon after his birth, when people chided Sayyidah Maryam on the basis of a false accusation, the newborn spoke up, saying *innī 'abdullāh* — "I am a servant of Allah." His first recorded sentence is a confession of servanthood.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites two narrations here, both from Abū Hurayrah. Muhammad bin Ishāq recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"No infant spoke in the cradle except 'Īsā and the companion of Jurayj."* And Ibn Abī Hātim recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"No infant spoke in the cradle except three: 'Īsā, the boy during the time of Jurayj, and another boy."*

**The puzzle of "kahl."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a question worth sitting with. Speaking in infancy is plainly a sign and a miracle, and it belongs in a list of marvels. But speaking to people during one's middle age is very normal — something everyone does, Muslim or not, learned or unlettered. Why is it mentioned here as something special?

One answer, Maʿārif reports, appears in *Bayān al-Qur'ān* by Maulana Ashraf Thanavi (may Allah have mercy on him): the real purpose is to focus on the miraculous nature of *meaningful* infant speech. The reference to speech in middle age is there to indicate that his childhood speech too would not be the usual baby-talk, but rational, even learned and eloquent, as a man speaks in his advanced years. The discussion then continues in the same breath: looking into the true historical background of 'Īsā (peace be upon him), this reference to him speaking to people in his middle age provides a great standing argument in favour of the Islamic position — that, according to Qur'anic belief, he has been raised alive onto the heavens. Hadith narrations, Maʿārif says, prove that when he was raised he was in the approximate age bracket of thirty to thirty-five, youth at its best. Middle age — *kahl* in Arabic — was something he never reached during his life in this world. So his talking to people in his middle age can happen only when he graces this world once again with his presence. Just as his childhood speech was a miracle, his speech in middle age could be nothing else but another miracle.

**"And he will be one of the righteous."** Ibn Kathir: righteous *in his statements and actions*, for he will possess pure knowledge and righteous works. Knowledge and deed together — a pairing that returns at the very end of this passage.

---

## Maryam's question, and the answer that guards her (47)

**"She said: 'O my Lord! How shall I have a son when no man has touched me.' He said: 'So (it will be), for Allah creates what He wills. When He has decreed something, He says to it only: Be! — and it is.'"**

Ibn Kathir puts her thought into words: *"How can I have a son while I did not marry, nor intend to marry, nor am I an indecent woman, may Allah forbid?"* Her question is not doubt about Allah's power; it is bewilderment about how, spoken by a woman whose whole life has been chastity. Maʿārif frames the same question a second way: was this to be a divine miracle, or would she be asked to marry a man? The divine answer eliminates the second possibility.

**"Allah creates what He wills."** Ibn Kathir: He is Mighty in power, and nothing escapes His ability. Maʿārif adds that His will alone is all-sufficient to bring something into existence — He needs no medium and no cause; it is only His command "Be" which makes things come into existence.

Then a detail of wording that repays attention. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah used the word **"create"** here instead of the word **"does,"** as in the account of Zakariyyā (3:40) — and the reason he gives is exact: *to eradicate any evil thought concerning 'Īsā.* A single verb, chosen to keep a shadow from ever falling on Maryam.

**"Be — and it is."** Ibn Kathir: what Allah wills comes into existence instantly and without delay. He brings in another ayah, *"And Our commandment is but one as the twinkling of an eye"* (54:50) — meaning, as he explains it, that the command is issued once and the thing comes into existence as fast as, and faster than, a blink of the eye.

---

## The education Allah gives, and the signs He sends with him (48–49)

**"And He will teach him the Book and Al-Hikmah, and the Tawrāh and the Injīl."**

Ibn Kathir notes that the "Book" mentioned here appears to refer to **writing**, and that he has already explained *Al-Hikmah* — wisdom — in his commentary on Sūrat al-Baqarah. The Tawrāh is the Book Allah sent down to Mūsā, son of 'Imrān; the Injīl is what Allah sent down to 'Īsā, son of Maryam, peace be upon them — and 'Īsā **memorised both Books**. Maʿārif reads ayah 48 as recounting his august virtues: born blessed with the honour of learning from Allah — Scripture, wisdom, and especially the Tawrāh and the Injīl — and then sent as a Messenger of Allah to all the Children of Israel.

The teaching flows straight into the mission. Maʿārif observes that the message he carries will itself be his argument in favour of his prophethood, and that the four signs enumerated in ayah 49 were enough for those willing to believe.

**"I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, that I design for you out of clay, a figure like that of a bird, and breathe into it, and it becomes a bird by Allah's leave; and I heal the blind, and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by Allah's leave. And I inform you of what you eat, and what you store in your houses. Surely, therein is a sign for you, if you believe."**

Ibn Kathir works through them. The clay bird: he used to make the shape of a bird from clay and blow into it, and it became a bird **by Allah's leave** — a miracle Allah made for him to testify that He had sent him. *Akmah*: Ibn Kathir specifies **a person who was born blind**, which, he says, perfects this miracle and makes the challenge more daring. The leper: "a known disease." And raising the dead — again, **by Allah's leave**. Then the last: telling a man what he has just eaten and what he is keeping in his house for tomorrow. All of these, Ibn Kathir says, are a sign testifying to the truth of what he was sent with.

**Why these signs?** Ibn Kathir reports that many scholars stated that Allah sent every Prophet with a miracle suitable to his time. In Mūsā's time, magic was the trade of the day and magicians held a high position — so Allah sent him with a miracle that captured the eyes and bewildered every magician, and when they realised it came from the Almighty, Most Great, they embraced Islam and became pious believers. 'Īsā was sent during a time when medicine and knowledge in physics were advancing — so he brought the kinds of miracles that could not be performed except by one sent by Allah. Ibn Kathir puts the challenge as a question: how can any physician bring life to clay, cure blindness and leprosy, and bring back to life those entrapped in the grave? And Muhammad ﷺ was sent during the time of eloquent people and proficient poets — so he brought them a Book from Allah such that if mankind and the jinn tried to imitate ten chapters of it, or even one chapter, they would utterly fail, even in collective cooperation; because the Qur'an is the Word of Allah and is nothing like that of the creatures.

**A ruling noted in passing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that making the shape of a bird was the making of a picture — something permitted in that Sharī'ah; in ours, its permissibility was abrogated.

---

## Confirming the old, and the one sentence he was sent to say (50–51)

**"(And I have come) confirming that which was before me of the Tawrāh, and to make lawful to you part of what was forbidden to you, and I have come to you with a proof from your Lord. So have Taqwā of Allah and obey me."**

Ibn Kathir: he came **affirming the Tawrāh and upholding it**. And the second half of the ayah indicates that 'Īsā abrogated some of the Laws of the Tawrāh and informed the Jews of the truth regarding some issues they used to dispute about — as another ayah says, *"And in order to make clear to you some of the points in which you differ"* (43:63). The proof from their Lord, Ibn Kathir explains, contained affirmation and evidence of the truth of what he was conveying.

Maʿārif spells out the same logic: the unlawfulness of some things in the earlier code would stand abrogated by the new one, and his station of prophethood was the conclusive argument for that claim of abrogation — with the signs from their Lord as the proof of his truth. *Taqwā* here — being on guard before Allah — is given its practical shape by Maʿārif: beware of any contravention of the divine commandments, fear Allah, and follow his teachings in matters of religion.

And then the last line, which the whole passage has been walking toward:

**"Truly, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him (Alone). This is the straight path."**

Ibn Kathir's comment is a single clause, and it settles everything before it: *for I and you are equal in our servitude, submission and humbleness to Him.* The one who healed the blind and raised the dead stands on the same ground as his listeners before Allah. And notice the order of his words: not "your Lord" alone, but **my** Lord first.

Maʿārif reads the ayah as the whole of religion in miniature: *"Allah is my Lord and your Lord"* is the ultimate in **belief**, and *"Worship Him"* is the ultimate in **deeds**. This, Maʿārif says, is the straight path — the path that perfects the ideal combination of beliefs and deeds, leads to the way of salvation, and is the source of communion with Allah.

---

## Living it

**Read the passage in the direction it moves.** Every honour named here is one 'Īsā (peace be upon him) *receives*: taught by Allah, honoured by Allah, sent by Allah, interceding **by Allah's leave**, healing **by Allah's leave**, raising the dead **by Allah's leave**. The passage lifts him as high as a human being goes — and then has him say, in his own voice, that Allah is his Lord as much as ours.

**Take Maryam's question as a model.** She asked *how*, not *whether*. There is a difference between a heart seeking to understand and a heart refusing to accept — and the answer she received, "Allah creates what He wills," is the answer to every impossibility a believer meets.

**Let "Be — and it is" reach your own affairs.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is that what Allah wills comes into existence instantly and without delay, faster than a blink. Nothing escapes His ability — not the child given to a mother with no husband, and not whatever you are carrying today.

**And the first words of that child.** Before any Scripture, before any miracle, the infant in the cradle said: *I am a servant of Allah.* That is the same claim ayah 51 ends with, and it is the one claim available to every one of us.

passages.title: The disciples' pledge and the plot against Jesus
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat capture the turning point in the mission of ʿĪsā (Jesus, peace be upon him): the moment he senses that his people have hardened against him, the moment a small band of sincere followers steps forward and declares its faith, and the moment his enemies move to destroy him — only to find that Allah's own move had already been made. What binds the passage together is a single contrast: the enemies' secret plotting on one side, and on the other a handful of believers who declare themselves helpers of Allah — and Allah Himself, who is "the Best of those who plot."

## The moment the mission changes

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Following the blessed predictions mentioned earlier in the sūrah, ʿĪsā was born with all the promised signs. As a messenger sent to Banī Isrāʼīl, he presented his call to them supported by miracles that proved his prophethood. But they were adamant. They kept on rejecting him as a prophet, even going to the limit of being physically hostile to him.

Ayah 52 opens with the words *fa-lammā aḥassa ʿĪsā* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "Then when ʿĪsā came to know" of their disbelief. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: ʿĪsā *felt* that they were adamant in disbelief and continuing in misguidance. This is not the discovery that some people disagreed with him; it is the settled recognition that a door has closed.

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easy to miss, and flags it under the heading "An Important Note." Ayah 52 states that ʿĪsā looked for helpers in the way of Allah **only when he sensed hostility from the disbelievers**, and not at the initial stage of his call. As is obvious, he had risen to the task all alone, obeying the command of his Lord, without worrying about setting up a "party" in advance. When the need came, he found a group around him. As Māʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, a little thought here would show that every worthy mission demands such determination and courage.

## "Who will be my helper in Allah's cause?"

The question in ayah 52 is *man anṣārī ilā Allāh*, which Ibn Kathir renders as "Who will be my helper in Allah's cause?"

The commentators read it in two ways. **Mujahid** commented: "Meaning, who would follow me to Allah?" — a call to join him on the road. **Ibn Kathir**, after reporting that, says that what appears more likely is that ʿĪsā was asking, "Who would help me convey the Message of Allah?" — a call for support in the work of conveying the message itself. The difference is whether the emphasis falls on following him or on carrying the message with him.

## The Prophet ﷺ asking the same question

Ibn Kathir places beside this ayah a scene from our own Prophet's ﷺ life, and it is the single most illuminating thing in his commentary on this passage. During the Hajj season, before the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Who will give me asylum so that I can convey the Speech of my Lord, for the Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the Speech of my Lord."

He kept asking until he found the Anṣār. They helped him and gave him refuge; he later migrated to them, and they comforted him and protected him from all his enemies — may Allah be pleased with them all.

(Ibn Kathir relates these words of the Prophet ﷺ without naming a ḥadīth collection, so the teaching stands as he reports it, without attribution to any named book.)

Ibn Kathir then says plainly: this is similar to what happened with ʿĪsā, for some of the Children of Israel believed in him, gave him their aid and support, and followed the light that was sent with him. The pattern is one pattern. A prophet is rejected by the many; he calls out for helpers; a few answer — and those few become the ones Allah names in His Book.

## Who were the ḥawāriyyūn?

Ibn Kathir gives the short answer: *ḥawārī* in Arabic means **support**.

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word further. *Ḥawāriyy* (singular of *al-ḥawāriyyūn*, translated as "the disciples") derives from **ḥawar**, which lexically means **whiteness**. In religious terminology the title was given to the sincere disciples or companions of ʿĪsā for one of three reasons: because of their sincerity, because of the purity of their hearts, or because of their white dress. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that, likewise, the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ have been called *ṣaḥābiyy* (plural *ṣaḥābah*).

Some commentators, Māʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, have given the number of the disciples as twelve. Incidentally, the word *ḥawāriyy* is also at times used in the absolute sense of "helper" or "supporter."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records from *the Two Ṣaḥīḥs* that when the Prophet ﷺ encouraged the people to fight during the battle of al-Aḥzāb, az-Zubayr came forward; and again, when the Prophet ﷺ asked for fighters a second time, az-Zubayr came forward. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Every Prophet has a ḥawārī, and az-Zubayr is my ḥawārī."

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same ḥadīth from *Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī*, glossing *ḥawārī* there as "a sincere companion." Note how the title was earned: the call for fighters went out, and the same man stepped forward both times.

## Their answer, and then their prayer

Their reply in ayah 52 is layered, and each layer matters.

**"We are the helpers of Allah."** The one they name in their answer is Allah.

**"We believe in Allah."** The support is built on belief.

**"And bear witness that we are Muslims."** They ask their prophet to be their witness — to testify on their behalf that they submitted.

Then ayah 53 turns the same content upward. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this structure explicit: the text identifies the very first followers of ʿĪsā and brings to light their real creed, "expressed first before their prophet and then (in verse 53), reiterated it in the form of a prayer before their Lord." The same declaration is made twice, to two different addressees — and only the second one is a duʿāʼ:

> "Our Lord! We believe in what You have sent down, and we follow the Messenger; so write us down among those who bear witness."

Notice the two halves. *We believe in what You have sent down* — assent to the revelation. *And we follow the Messenger* — following the one who brought it. Faith and following, never separated.

Then the request: **"so write us down among those who bear witness"** (*fa-ktubnā maʿa ash-shāhidīn*). Having just asked ʿĪsā to bear witness *for* them, they ask Allah to write them down *among the witnesses*.

**Ibn ʿAbbās on this phrase.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said of "so write us down among those who bear witness": *"Meaning among the Ummah of Muḥammad."* Ibn Kathir adds that this "has a good chain of narration." Read that way, the first sincere followers of ʿĪsā prayed to be enrolled in the community of the Prophet ﷺ who had not yet come — a striking thing for a reader of this sūrah to sit with.

## Ayah 54: *makr*, and what the word really means

"And they plotted, and Allah planned too. And Allah is the Best of those who plot."

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah with unusual care over the language, and explains why the care is necessary. The Arabic word **makr** denotes *a subtle and secret move or plan*. If it is for a good purpose it is good; if it is for a bad purpose it is bad. That is exactly why the qualifier *sayyiʼ* (evil) was placed alongside *makr* in the verse *"And evil plan besets none but its perpetrator"* (35:43).

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution that speaks directly to non-Arabic readers: in the everyday idiom of Urdu — the language in which the commentary was originally written — the word *makr* is used exclusively for conspiracy, evil plan and strategy, and therefore should not be equated with the Arabic usage. This, the commentary says, is the reason why Allah has been called here **Khayr al-Mākirīn**, "the Best of those who make moves."

So, on Māʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, the parallel wording is not attributing the enemies' evil scheming to Allah. The ayah tells us that while the Jews were setting one thing in motion in secret, "the subtle and secret move made by Allah Almighty was countering their evil plans more effectively" — and Māʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this counter-move is what the following verses go on to describe.

## The plot itself

Ibn Kathir tells the story. The Children of Israel tried to kill ʿĪsā by conspiring to defame him and crucify him. They complained about him to the king, who was a disbeliever, claiming that ʿĪsā was a man who misguided people, discouraged them from obeying the king, caused division, and separated between a man and his own son. They also said other lies about him — lies which, as Ibn Kathir says, they will carry on their necks — including accusing him of being an illegitimate son. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Jews' conspiracies went to the limit of convincing the ruler of the time that ʿĪsā was a heretic, bent upon changing the Torah and about to make apostates of everybody.

The king became furious and sent his men to capture ʿĪsā, to torture and crucify him. They surrounded his home, and he thought that they would surely capture him.

Then Allah saved him from them. Ibn Kathir relates that Allah raised him up from the house to heaven, and put the image of ʿĪsā on a man who was in the house. When the unjust people went into the house while it was still dark, they thought that he was ʿĪsā. They captured that man, humiliated him and crucified him, and placed thorns on his head. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same account in brief: they sent one of them to arrest ʿĪsā, Allah changed that man's face totally and made him resemble ʿĪsā, ʿĪsā was raised to the heavens, and that person was crucified under the mistaken identity.

Ibn Kathir's conclusion is stark: Allah saved and raised His Prophet away from them, leaving them in disarray in the darkness of their transgression, thinking that they had successfully achieved their goal. Allah made their hearts hard and defiant of the truth, disgracing them with a disgrace that will remain with them until the Day of Resurrection. *And they plotted, and Allah planned too. And Allah is the Best of those who plot.*

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that how Allah had planned to save ʿĪsā from their clutches was disclosed to him when his enemies came to arrest him, and that the details of those disclosures are mentioned in verse 55.

## Why the wording is explained so carefully

Māʿārif ul Qurʼān states its reason plainly. Some sects deny — "contrary to the belief of the entire Muslim community" — the ascension of ʿĪsā, his being alive in the heavens, and his descent in the later times, and they have worked through the words and meanings of these verses to open doors of distortion in the Qur'anic text. That is why, the commentary says, it seemed appropriate to explain these words in some detail.

## Living it

**Start alone if you must.** ʿĪsā did not build a following before beginning; he rose to the task alone in obedience to the command of his Lord, and when the need came he found a group around him. Māʿārif ul Qurʼān names this as the lesson of the ayah's timing: every worthy mission demands such determination and courage.

**Answer when the call goes out.** Az-Zubayr's title was earned by coming forward at al-Aḥzāb when the Prophet ﷺ called for fighters — and again when he called a second time. The ḥawāriyyūn came forward at a comparable moment: after ʿĪsā had sensed the hostility of his people.

**Say it to Allah, not only to people.** The disciples declared their faith before their prophet and then, in ayah 53, said the same thing again to their Lord as a prayer. A commitment announced publicly is worth little until it has been placed before Allah.

**Ask to be written down.** Their duʿāʼ in ayah 53 is a beautiful one to carry: *Rabbanā āmannā bimā anzalta wa-t-tabaʿnā ar-rasūla fa-ktubnā maʿa ash-shāhidīn* — "Our Lord! We believe in what You have sent down, and we follow the Messenger; so write us down among those who bear witness."

**And when the plotting closes in.** The last words of ayah 54 are meant to be a believer's rest. Whatever is being arranged in secret against the truth, Allah's own move is subtler still and counters it more effectively — and Allah is the Best of those who plot.

passages.title: Allah's promise to Jesus and the two outcomes
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat record what Allah said to ʿĪsā (Jesus, peace be upon him) at a time when the Jews were bent on killing him — a promise in five parts — and then how that promise ends: two outcomes for two kinds of people, sealed by a statement that all of this is revelation.

What holds them together is one line of thought. Ayah 55 is Allah's speech to ʿĪsā; ayat 56 and 57 continue that same speech, telling him in advance how the dispute over him will be settled; ayah 58 turns to the Prophet ﷺ and certifies the account. The passage moves from **rescue**, to **verdict**, to **certification**.

## The moment being recalled

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these words against the ayah just before them — "And they made a move, and Allah made a move." The Jews had resolved to crucify and kill ʿĪsā. Allah made the sinister move of his enemies recoil upon those who had gone into the house to kill him: one of them was changed to look exactly like ʿĪsā, and ʿĪsā himself was raised alive to the heavens. So ayah 55 is not abstract doctrine dropped into the sūrah; it is comfort spoken to a prophet under threat of death.

## "I will take you in full" — the word *mutawaffīka*

Everything here turns on one word. *Mutawaffīka* comes from the verbal noun *tawaffī*, root *wafyun*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that its lexical meaning — universally confirmed by all lexicons of the Arabic language — is **"to take in full"**; its derivations *wafā'*, *īfā'* and *istīfā'* are used to convey that same sense. Death is a *figurative*, derived use: a man completes his appointed time at the hour of death, and the soul Allah gave him is taken back fully and conclusively. Sleep is a simpler form of the same taking, which is why the Qur'an uses this very word of it: "Allah takes away lives of the living at the time of their death and of those that do not die, in their sleep" (39:42).

Two authorities are quoted:

- **Ibn Taymiyyah**, in *al-Jawāb al-Ṣaḥīḥ*: *al-tawaffī*, in the Arabic language, means to exact fully or take in full, and it takes three forms — to take in sleep, to take in death, and to take the soul and the body all together.
- **Kulliyāt Abī al-Baqā'**: *al-tawaffī* is putting to death and exacting of the soul in common usage, while in the classical usage it is taking in full and the exacting of the due right.

On that basis Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that **the majority of scholars** have translated *mutawaffīka* here in the sense of "taking in full": Allah will not leave ʿĪsā in the hands of the Jews — rather He would take him away, and that taking would be in the form of his being raised unto Him in the heavens.

**Ibn Kathīr** reads it differently, glossing "I will take you and raise you to Myself" as *while you are asleep*, comparing 6:60 ("It is He Who takes your souls by night") and 39:42. He notes that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite these words when he would awaken: *"All the thanks are due to Allah Who brought us back to life after He had caused us to die (sleep), and the Return is to Him"* — sleep called a death, waking a return to life. Ibn Kathīr adds that Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from **al-Ḥasan** that "I will take you" is in reference to sleep, for Allah raised ʿĪsā while he was asleep.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a third reading: some authentic commentators have interpreted these words in the sense of **giving death** — but they do not mean that his death will occur at the hands of his enemies. On this reading Allah said two things to comfort ʿĪsā at a time when the Jews were bent on killing him: that his death would come as a natural death and not at their hands, and that in order to rescue him from their evil designs Allah would at that time raise him towards Himself. Maʿārif states that this explanation is exactly what has been reported from **Ibn ʿAbbās**, as quoted by al-Suyūṭī in *al-Durr al-Manthūr* on the authority of several narrators.

## Why "death" is mentioned before "raising"

If *tawaffī* here carries the sense of death, a difficulty appears — the raising happened first, and the death has not yet happened. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that there is an element of precedence and sequence in the words used. *Wa rāfiʿuka* (I shall raise you) comes first in time; *mutawaffīka* (I shall give you death) comes later — and mentioning the later one earlier is itself a hint about events still to come. It means that the raising towards Allah will not last forever: it would be temporary, and then he would return to the mortal world, prevail over his enemies, and later on die a natural death.

The wisdom in that word order repays a pause. His return from heaven and his death after having established his victory were not only a miracle but a consummation of his honour and integrity — and, in addition, a refutation of the unfounded belief in his divinity. Had the ayah not been worded this way, his being raised alive into the heavens could have further strengthened the false belief that he too was Living and Eternal like Allah. By introducing the word pointing to his death first, all such misconceptions were refuted in advance. Imām al-Rāzī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, has said that such precedence and sequence — an event due later mentioned first for some expedient consideration — occurs frequently in the noble Qur'an (*al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr*, v. 2, p. 48).

## "And raise you to Myself"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. ʿĪsā is not the name of just the spirit, but of the spirit *and* the body. To take the raising in the sense that it was spiritual only, and not physical, is therefore all wrong. It is true that *rafʿ* (raising) is sometimes used of rank — "And raised some of you in ranks over others" (6:165); "and Allah will raise up in rank those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge" (58:11). But in those places the sense of rank is figurative, fixed by their own contexts, and there is no reason here to ignore the real meaning and go by the figurative. Decisively, this ayah says *rāfiʿuka **ilayya*** — "I shall raise you **towards Me**" — and using *ilā* alongside *rafʿ* at this particular place totally eliminates the possibility of a figurative meaning. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the same construction in 4:158, which it renders: "the Jews certainly did not kill Jesus... instead, Allah raised him towards Himself." That later expression, it concludes, is used for nothing but the raising alive of the spirit and the body. We affirm "towards Me" as Allah has stated it, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying His words of their meaning.

## Five promises in one ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts five promises made to ʿĪsā in ayah 55, all of them concerning the Jews:

**1.** His death **will not come at the hands of the Jews** through killing. It will be a natural death coming at its appointed time, and that appointed time will come close to the Day of Doom, when he will come down from the heavens onto the earth — as reported in detail, Maʿārif says, in sound aḥādīth transmitted through unbroken chains.

**2.** He will be **raised towards the heavens** in the existing situation — fulfilled right then. Maʿārif cites the report of that fulfilment in Sūrah al-Nisā' (4:158): "Certainly, the Jews did not kill him, instead; Allah Almighty raised him towards Himself."

**3.** *"And purify you from those who disbelieve"* — to have him cleansed of the false accusations brought on him by his enemies. Ibn Kathīr reads this purification as *by raising you to heaven*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as fulfilled when the last of the prophets came and refuted all the false accusations: they threw slanders on his parentage because he was born without a father, and the Qur'an answered that this was Allah's power and will — and less surprising than the birth of Ādam, who was born without both a father and a mother. They accused him of claiming to be God, and there are many ayat in which, contrary to that accusation, ʿĪsā is reported to have publicly confessed his being human and a servant and bondsman of Allah.

**4.** *"And placed those who follow you above those who disbelieve"* — his followers will be made to overcome those who deny and oppose him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains "following" here as belief in and confession of his prophethood; belief in and practice of all the injunctions ascribed to him is not a precondition for *this* promise, which is why both Christians and Muslims fall in this category as regards worldly dominance over the Jews. But the tafsīr is emphatic that holding this much of belief is not enough to bring salvation in the Hereafter. That depends on believing in all the injunctions ʿĪsā brought — and one of his instructions was that his followers should believe in the last of the Prophets ﷺ, who would come after him. The Christians did not follow that instruction; the Muslims acted in accordance with it.

Ibn Kathīr traces the same promise through history. When Allah raised ʿĪsā to heaven, his followers divided into sects: some believed in what Allah sent him as — a servant of Allah, His Messenger, and the son of His female servant — while others went to the extreme, saying he was the son of Allah, or Allah Himself, or one of a Trinity. His religion was then changed by Constantine, who added to it and deleted from it. When Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ, those who believed in him were the true followers of every Prophet, and Allah abrogated the earlier laws with the Law He sent him with — the true religion that shall never change or be altered until the commencement of the Last Hour. Ibn Kathīr's conclusion is striking: **Muslims are the true believers in ʿĪsā.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that a temporary domination by the Jews close to the Day of Judgment has itself been reported in the authentic reports of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, so such a domination would not be contrary to the reports Muslims consider authentic.

**5.** The **final verdict** — "Then, to Me is your return, whereupon I shall judge between you" (3:55) — will certainly be fulfilled at its appointed time.

## Alive, and returning

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the Muslim position against two others. The Jews are the only people who say that ʿĪsā was crucified, killed and buried, and never returned to life. The Christians say he was indeed killed on the cross, but was brought back to life and raised to the heavens. The Qur'an answers both with *shubbiha lahum* — "And they did not kill him and they did not crucify him, but they were deluded by resemblance" (4:157). Both fell for the same mistaken identity: the Jews rejoiced after killing their own man, and the Christians built their belief on the same error.

The Islamic belief is that Allah raised him alive onto the heavens in order to rescue him from the Jews; he was not to be killed and not to be crucified; he is in the heavens alive; and close to the Day of Judgment he will come down from the heavens, lead the Muslims to victory over the Jews, and finally die a natural death. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports **the consensus of the entire Muslim community** on this belief, recorded by Ibn Ḥajar in *Talkhīṣ al-Ḥabīr* (p. 319), resting on several ayat of the Qur'an and on *mutawātir* aḥādīth — reports transmitted through an unbroken chain of reporting. Ibn Kathīr, commenting on 43:61, likewise says that there are aḥādīth from the Holy Prophet ﷺ narrated in uninterrupted succession that he proclaimed the coming of ʿĪsā before the Day of Judgment **as a just leader**.

**Why the Qur'an gives ʿĪsā such detail.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an observation worth sitting with. In this sūrah, Ādam, Nūḥ, the family of Ibrāhīm and the family of ʿImrān are referred to briefly in a single ayah — while nearly three sections and twenty-two ayat go to ʿĪsā and his family with meticulous detail: his grandmother and her pledge, his mother's birth, name and upbringing, the conception, the birth, the blames and curses of her people, the newborn's eloquence, his call and his disciples, the hostile attempts to trap and kill him, and his being raised alive. Such detail has not been given in that manner even in respect of the Last of the prophets ﷺ. Why? Because, the tafsīr answers, being the final prophet with no apostle to come after him, he took special care to identify for his community both those worthy of being followed and those who posed a danger to its faith. He related many details of the Dajjāl's profile and traits so that no room for doubt would remain when he appears; by the same logic the community had to be given the clearest indications of ʿĪsā's person and qualities — for should the community find it difficult to identify him, the very purpose of his coming would be negated. Maʿārif adds that these indicators also serve to refute false claimants, as the scholars of the Muslim community used them to refute the claim of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian.

## The two outcomes (ayat 56–57)

The promise now resolves into a verdict with two branches.

For those who disbelieve: *"a severe torment in this world and in the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers."* Ibn Kathīr applies this to the Jews who disbelieved in ʿĪsā and the Christians who went to the extreme over him — tormented in this life, killed, captured, and stripped of their wealth and kingdoms, with a torment in the Hereafter that is even worse and more severe, and no defender or protector against Allah (13:34).

For those who believe and do righteous deeds: *"Allah will pay them their reward in full."* Ibn Kathīr says this is paid in this life with victory and domination, and in the Hereafter with Paradise and high grades. Notice the verb — *yuwaffīhim*, from the same root *wafy* that opened the passage in *mutawaffīka*. The One who **takes in full** is the One who **pays in full**.

**A puzzle, and its answer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a fair question: the judgment here relates to the Last Day, so how can ayah 56 say "in this world and in the Hereafter" when this world will not exist at that time? The answer offered is a courtroom analogy. A judge tells a culprit, *"Right now I am sending you to the jail for a year; if you misbehave there, I shall make it for two years"* — meaning the two years are counted from the day the punishment is awarded. So too here: the punishment in the world has already been given, the punishment of the Hereafter is added on, and the sum-total is finally executed on the Last Day.

The consequence is sobering. **Having been punished in this world will not serve as expiation for the punishment of the Hereafter.** For the believer it is the opposite: when believers are struck by suffering in the mortal world, their sins are forgiven and the punishment due in the Hereafter is lightened or warded off. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds the hint for this in the closing clause of ayah 57 — *"And Allah does not like the wrongdoers."* Believers are dear because of their belief, and the beloved are always treated in such a manner; the disbelievers are detested because of their disbelief, and those detested do not receive such treatment. (Bayān al-Qur'an)

## Ayah 58: the seal

*"This is what We recite to you of the verses and the Wise Reminder."*

Ibn Kathīr's paraphrase: what We narrated to you, O Muḥammad, regarding ʿĪsā, his birth and his life, is what Allah conveyed and revealed to you, sent down from *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ*, the Preserved Tablet — **so there is no doubt in it.** He points to the matching seal in Sūrah Maryam: "Such is ʿĪsā, son of Maryam. (It is) a statement of truth, about which they doubt (or dispute). It befits not Allah that He should beget a son. Glorified be He. When He decrees a thing, He only says to it: 'Be!' and it is."

That is why the passage closes where it does. Ayat 55–57 are not one more tradition to be set beside those of the People of the Book and weighed. They are among the *āyāt* — the signs — and *al-dhikr al-ḥakīm*, the Wise Reminder: an account whose authority is that Allah is its reciter.

## Living it

**Take the comfort of ayah 55 personally.** A prophet stood surrounded by people who had already decided to kill him, and Allah's answer was not to empty the room of danger but to tell him how it ends. Being cornered is not the same as being abandoned.

**Hold ʿĪsā where the Qur'an holds him.** Ibn Kathīr's phrase is the standard: a servant of Allah, His Messenger, and the son of His female servant — no less, and no more. The two errors named in this passage run in opposite directions, and both are ruinous: denying him, and going to the extreme over him.

**Take *yuwaffīhim* at its word.** Allah pays the reward *in full*. Whatever of your work goes unseen, unthanked and unrecorded by anyone else is on an account that will be settled in full.

passages.title: Jesus likened to Adam and the mubahala challenge
passages.tafsir:
# Jesus likened to Adam, and the challenge of Mubāhala (3:59–63)

This passage brings the Qur'an's long discussion of 'Isa (Jesus, peace be upon him) to its conclusion with two moves. First a proof: a birth without a father shows Allah's power, not the divinity of the one born (ayah 59). Then, when argument has done all it can do, a challenge: if you still dispute after knowledge has reached you, let us stand together before Allah and ask that His curse fall on whichever side is lying (ayah 61). The unit closes by naming what has just been said as *the* true account, and warning that walking away from a truth this clear is not neutrality but corruption (ayat 62–63).

## The occasion: the delegation from Najrān

Ibn Kathīr reports, on the authority of Imām Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Yasār and other scholars, that the reason for the call to Mubāhala — and for the revelation of this Sūrah from its beginning down to these ayat — was that a delegation of Christians from Najrān (in Yemen) came to Madinah to argue about 'Isa, claiming he was divine and the son of Allah.

Ibn Ishāq describes them in his famous *Sīrah*: sixty horsemen, including fourteen of their chiefs who made decisions. Three men led them — Al-'Āqib, also called 'Abd al-Masīh, their leader and the one they turned to for advice and decision; As-Sayyid, also called Al-Ayham, their scholar and their leader on journeys and at gatherings; and Abū Hārithah ibn 'Alqamah, their patriarch, priest and religious leader. Abū Hārithah was an Arab of Bakr ibn Wā'il, but when he embraced Christianity the Romans and their kings honoured him, built churches for him, supported him financially and gave him servants, because they knew how firm his faith in their religion was.

Then Ibn Kathīr adds a detail that should stop any reader: **Abū Hārithah knew the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from what he had read in the earlier divine Books.** Yet, Ibn Kathīr says, his ignorance in other respects led him to insist on remaining a Christian — and he did so because he was honoured and held a high position among the Christians. Two things are named together, then: what he still did not understand, and what he stood to lose.

Ibn Ishāq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Az-Zubayr, describes their arrival: they entered the Prophet's ﷺ masjid in Madinah wearing robes and garments after he ﷺ had prayed 'Asr, accompanying a caravan of camels led by Banū Al-Hārith ibn Ka'b. The Companions who saw them said they never saw a delegation like them after that.

And they were not one voice. Ibn Ishāq records that they disagreed about 'Isa among themselves: some said "He is Allah," some said "He is the son of Allah," and some said "He is one of a trinity." Allah is far above what they attribute to Him.

Ibn Kathīr takes each claim in turn. They called him God because he brought the dead back to life, healed blindness and leprosy and various illnesses, told of matters of the future, and shaped birds and blew life into them — yet all of these miracles occurred *by Allah's leave*, so that 'Isa would be a sign from Allah for people. They called him the son of Allah because he had no father and spoke while in the cradle. They spoke of a trinity because Allah says "We did, We commanded, We created" — arguing that if Allah were one He would have said "I." Allah is far above what they attribute to Him, and, as Ibn Kathīr notes, the Qur'an has refuted every one of these claims.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān gives the political frame: the Holy Prophet ﷺ had put three options to the Christians of Najrān, in this order — accept Islam, or pay *jizya* (a levy on free non-Muslims under Muslim rule), or get ready for war. After mutual consultation they sent a delegation (Ma'ārif names Shurahbīl, 'Abdullāh ibn Shurahbīl and Jabbār ibn Fayd) which came and began talks on religious issues. It was when they pushed their effort to prove the godhood of 'Isa to the extremes of dispute that the ayah of Mubāhala came down. (The two accounts name different men among the delegation; Ma'ārif's summary is offered as it stands, alongside Ibn Ishāq's fuller list.)

## Ayah 59: "the likeness of 'Isa is the likeness of Adam"

Ibn Kathīr is precise about *what* the comparison compares. The likeness of 'Isa "before Allah" concerns **Allah's ability** — He created him without a father. And the likeness of Adam is this: Allah created him without a father *or* a mother, from dust, then said to him "Be!" and he was.

The logic is a trap that closes gently. The One who created Adam without a father or a mother is certainly able to create 'Isa without a father. And if the claim is made that 'Isa is Allah's son because he was created without a father, then the same claim befits Adam even more — he had neither. But such a claim about Adam is obviously false. So, Ibn Kathīr says, making the same claim about 'Isa is even more false. The very feature they lean on becomes the thing that dismantles their conclusion.

Ibn Kathīr then widens the lens. By mentioning these facts, Allah emphasises His ability: Adam created without a male or female, Hawwā' from a male without a female, 'Isa from a mother without a father — compared with His creating the rest of creation from male and female. Four possibilities, all of them His. This is why Allah said of 'Isa in Sūrah Maryam, *"And We made him a sign for mankind"* (19:21). A sign points beyond itself. To worship the sign is to miss what it was pointing at.

## Ayah 60: "so do not be one of those who doubt"

Ibn Kathīr's gloss is stark: this is *the only* true story about 'Isa — and what is beyond truth save falsehood? Then, he notes, Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to call those who defy the truth regarding 'Isa to the Mubāhala.

That is the shape of the ayah. The truth about 'Isa has come "from your Lord" — not as one opinion among several, but as settled ground you stand on while others argue.

## Ayah 61: the Mubāhala

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān explains the term. *Mubāhala* literally means "mutual prayer"; in the terminology of the Islamic Sharī'ah it refers to a particular form of resolving religious disputes. When the argumentation from both sides fails to resolve a religious issue, the two parties jointly pray to Allah to cast His curse on whichever of them is false. And since a curse means *moving someone far away from the divine mercy* — and to be far from mercy is to be close to divine wrath — the essence of the meaning is: *wrath be on the liar.* Whoever is the liar shall face the evil consequences, whereupon the truth becomes evident even to those who rejected it.

Notice how carefully the ayah is worded. It is not "call your curse down upon you." It is "**we** pray and **we** invoke Allah's curse upon **the liars**" — Ibn Kathīr adds: "among the two of us." Both parties put themselves under the same judgement. Nobody is exempt. That is what makes it terrifying, and that is what makes it honest: only someone certain of his truthfulness would ever propose it.

Ma'ārif notes that, originally, a Mubāhala can be carried out by the disputants alone — they may simply get together and pray, and it is not necessary that all their family members are assembled. However, if the family members do participate, it becomes more effective. That is why the Holy Prophet ﷺ was instructed to invite the family members of both sides. And that is the weight of "our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves": each side stakes not only itself but everything it loves most.

**Who came out.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records that the Holy Prophet ﷺ came out quite readily for the Mubāhala, bringing with him Sayyidah Fātimah, Sayyidnā 'Alī, and their sons Hasan and Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them. Seeing this, Ma'ārif continues, Shurahbīl said to his two comrades: "Look, you already know that he is a prophet of Allah, and getting into a Mubāhala confrontation with a prophet means certain death and destruction for us. So find out some other way to get out of this fix." They asked him what he had in mind. He said the best solution was to opt for the truce the Prophet ﷺ had advised — and on this everybody agreed.

**A point on the word "sons."** Ma'ārif explains that "our sons" in ayah 61 does not mean sons of one's own loins only; the sense is general, covering sons and grandsons, because this is how the word is used in common usage. So Hasan and Husayn, the Prophet's ﷺ grandsons, and 'Alī, his son-in-law, are all included in "our sons" — and 'Alī has a further reason for inclusion, since he had grown up under the patronage of the Prophet ﷺ, who treated him like his own son. Ma'ārif raises this because some Shī'ites have claimed that 'Alī, not being a son, could not be referred to as "our son," and have concluded from that that he fell under "ourselves" and was therefore the immediate successor of the Prophet ﷺ. Ma'ārif holds that the ordinary wider usage of "sons" is enough to show the fallacy of that argument.

## What actually happened

Ibn Ishāq continues the story. When these ayat came, judging between the Prophet ﷺ and the People of the Book, Allah commanded him ﷺ to call them to the Mubāhala if they still refused the truth. He ﷺ called them to it. They said, "O Abū al-Qāsim, let us think about this matter and get back to you with our decision." They left and conferred with Al-'Āqib, to whom they referred for advice: "O 'Abd al-Masīh, what is your advice?" His answer is one of the most revealing speeches in the whole episode: "By Allah, O Christian fellows! You know that Muhammad is a Messenger and that he brought you the final word regarding your fellow ('Isa). You also know that no Prophet conducted Mubāhala with any people, and the old persons among them remained safe and the young people grew up. Indeed, it will be the end of you if you do it. If you have already decided that you will remain in your religion and your creed regarding your fellow, then conduct a treaty with the man and go back to your land."

So they returned and said: we cannot do Mubāhala with you; you remain on your religion and we remain on ours. However, send with us a man from your Companions whom you are pleased with, to judge between us regarding our monetary disputes — for you are acceptable to us in *that*.

They knew. Their own leader said it aloud. And still they chose the treaty over the truth, because the treaty let them keep everything except the one thing that mattered.

Al-Bukhārī records that Hudhayfah said: Al-'Āqib and As-Sayyid, two leaders from Najrān, came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ seeking to invoke Allah for curses, and one said to the other, "Let us not do that. By Allah, if he were truly a Prophet and we invoke Allah for curses, we and our offspring shall never succeed afterwards."

Imām Ahmad records from Ibn 'Abbās that when Abū Jahl said he would step on the Prophet's ﷺ neck if he saw him praying next to the Ka'bah, the Prophet ﷺ said: had he tried to do it, the angels would have taken him publicly; had the Jews wished for death, they would have perished and would have seen their seats in the Fire; and had those who sought Mubāhala with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gone ahead with it, they would not have found estates or families when they returned home. Ibn Kathīr notes that Al-Bukhārī, At-Tirmidhī and An-Nasā'ī also recorded this hadith, which At-Tirmidhī graded *Hasan Sahīh*.

## The trustee of this Ummah

In that same narration of Hudhayfah recorded by Al-Bukhārī, they said, "We will give you what you asked, and send a trusted man with us, just a trusted man." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Verily, I will send a trusted man with you, a truly trustworthy man." The Companions all felt eager to be that man. He ﷺ said, "O Abū 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrāh, stand up." When Abū 'Ubaydah stood, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "This is the trustee of this Ummah." Al-Bukhārī also records from Anas that he ﷺ said on another occasion: "Every Ummah has a trustee, and the trustee of this Ummah is Abū 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrāh."

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds that the outcome was peace: the Holy Prophet ﷺ made peace by fixing a levy on them, which they accepted.

## Ayat 62–63: the verdict

"Verily, this is the true narrative" — Ibn Kathīr: what We narrated to you, O Muhammad, about 'Isa is the plain truth that cannot be avoided. Everything else circulating about him is a story; this is *the* account.

Then the conclusion the whole passage has been building toward: "and none has the right to be worshipped but Allah." The argument about 'Isa was never merely historical. It was about who is worshipped. "And indeed, Allah is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise."

Ayah 63 handles the ones who simply turn away. Turning away, Ibn Kathīr says, means abandoning this truth — and those who abandon the truth for falsehood commit mischief. Allah has full knowledge of them and will subject them to the worst punishment. Ibn Kathīr closes his commentary here with a believer's own posture: Allah is able to control everything, all praise and thanks are due to Him, and we seek refuge with Him from His revenge.

## Living it

**Argue, but know where argument ends.** Ma'ārif records that the delegation came and began talks on religious issues; it was only when they pushed the dispute to its extremes that the ayah of Mubāhala was revealed. Evidence first; the appeal to Allah is not the opening move.

**Watch what makes people refuse the truth.** Abū Hārithah had read the description of the Messenger ﷺ in the earlier divine Books — yet Ibn Kathīr names both his remaining ignorance and the honour and high position he held among the Christians as what kept him a Christian. Al-'Āqib told his own people, by Allah, that Muhammad ﷺ is a Messenger, and still advised a treaty so that they could remain in their religion. It is worth asking honestly what we are protecting when we resist something we already suspect is true.

**Certainty is not the same as loudness.** The Prophet ﷺ answered the challenge by coming out quite readily with the people dearest to him — his daughter, his grandsons, 'Alī — all set for the Mubāhala. That is what conviction looks like when it costs something.

**Do not be one of the doubters.** Ayah 60 is the instruction that outlives the event: the truth about 'Isa came *from your Lord*. Hold it as ground, not as an opinion still open for negotiation.

passages.title: A common word and the claim to Abraham
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These five ayat are the closing move of a long argument with the People of the Book. In ayah 64 the Prophet ﷺ is told to issue an invitation — come to the one thing we can all stand on: that Allah alone is worshipped. Then, in ayat 65–68, the Qur'an dismantles the tug-of-war over Ibrahim (peace be upon him), in which Jews and Christians each claimed him for their own community, and settles the question of who really has a claim on him.

What holds the passage together is a single idea: **religion is not ancestry or label, it is submission to Allah alone.** Ayah 64 states that principle as an invitation; ayat 65–68 prove it from the life of the man both sides revered most.

---

## The setting: the delegation of Najran

Ibn Kathir reports that Muhammad bin Ishaq and other scholars said the beginning of Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān, and more than eighty verses thereafter, were revealed about the delegation of Najran, which came to Al-Madinah.

For ayat 65–68 specifically, Ibn Kathir records that Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said: *"The Christians of Najran and Jewish rabbis gathered before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and disputed in front of him. The rabbis said, 'Ibrahim was certainly Jewish.' The Christians said, 'Certainly, Ibrahim was Christian.'"* And so Allah sent down ayah 65.

Picture the scene: two groups who agreed on almost nothing, standing in front of the Prophet ﷺ, each insisting that Ibrahim belonged to them. That is the moment this passage answers.

---

## Ayah 64: "Come to a word"

**Who is addressed.** Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah includes the People of the Book — the Jews and Christians — and those who follow their ways.

**"Word" here means a whole statement.** Ibn Kathir points out that *"Word" — in Arabic — also means a complete sentence, "as evident from this Ayah."* So the invitation is not to a slogan but to a full proposition, which the ayah itself then spells out.

**A word that is *sawāʾ* between us and you.** Ibn Kathir explains this as "an honest and righteous word that is fair to both parties." It is common ground offered on equal terms — something neither side can honestly reject, because both already claim to hold it.

The ayah then breaks the "word" into three clauses:

**1. "That we worship none but Allah."** Ibn Kathir writes: "we worship neither a statue, cross, idol, Ṭāghūt (false gods), fire or anything else. Rather, we worship Allah Alone without partners." He adds that this is "the message of all of Allah's Messengers," citing Allah's words: *"And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me"* (21:25), and *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger: Worship Allah alone, and avoid Ṭāghūt"* (16:36). **Ṭāghūt**, as Ibn Kathir glosses it here, means false gods — all false deities.

**2. "And that we associate no partners with Him."** Pure worship, with nothing admitted alongside it.

**3. "And that none of us shall take others as lords besides Allah."** This is the clause people find hardest to place. Ibn Kathir preserves the comment of Ibn Jurayj: **"We do not obey each other in disobedience to Allah."** So taking someone as a "lord" does not require bowing to him. It happens when a human being's word is allowed to override Allah's — when a person is followed into what Allah has forbidden. This is a warning aimed at every community, including our own, which is why the ayah says *baʿḍunā baʿḍan* — "some of **us**," not "some of you."

**"Then, if they turn away, say: Bear witness that we are Muslims."** Ibn Kathir explains: if they abandon this fair call, "then let them know that you will remain in Islam as Allah has legislated for you."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a practical lesson from this closing line: when someone refuses to accept the truth even after it has been proved clearly, the proper course is to re-state one's own belief and conclude the conversation. "Entering into further debate and verbal altercation is not appropriate." The ayah teaches a believer how to *stop* arguing without conceding anything.

---

## The letter to Heraclius

Both commentaries connect this ayah to the Prophet's ﷺ letter to Heraclius, the Byzantine ruler. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the letter from Al-Bukhari:

> "I begin with the name of Allah who is All-Merciful, Very-Merciful. From Muhammad, servant of Allah, and His messenger: To Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor. Peace be on him who takes the right path… I invite you to the call of Islam. Embrace Islam and be in peace. Allah will bestow upon you a twofold reward, but should you turn away, then, on you shall be the sin of your subjects."

And then, word for word, this very ayah.

**The da'wah principle.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the method: someone who desires to carry his call to a group holding different beliefs should "induce that group to unite only on what they both can agree to." The Prophet ﷺ picked a particular point on which there was mutual agreement — the Oneness of Allah Almighty — and built from there. Notice, too, that nothing is conceded: the letter is an unambiguous call to Islam. Common ground is a *starting* point, not a substitute for the message.

**A chronological puzzle, and Ibn Kathir's answer.** Ibn Kathir raises a difficulty worth following, because it shows how carefully the scholars handled history. Muhammad bin Ishaq says these verses came down about the Najran delegation. Az-Zuhri states that the people of Najran were the first to pay the Jizyah (tax money paid to the Muslim State) — yet there is no disagreement that the ayah ordaining the Jizyah (9:29) was revealed *after* the conquest of Makkah, while the letter to Heraclius containing 3:64 was sent *before* it. How do these fit?

Ibn Kathir answers on two fronts. First, the delegation of Najran came before Al-Hudaybiyyah, and what they paid was in lieu of the *Mubāhalah*, not as Jizyah; the Jizyah ayah was revealed later, and its ruling supported what had already occurred with the people of Najran. Second, it is possible that the Prophet ﷺ wrote this statement in his letter to Heraclius *before* the ayah was revealed, and the Qur'an later came down agreeing with his statement word by word. Ibn Kathir cites parallels: the ruling on dividing the booty into one-fifth and four-fifths agreed with the practice of ʿAbdullah bin Jahsh during the raid he led before Badr; and the Qur'an was revealed in agreement with what ʿUmar said regarding the captured disbelievers at Badr, the *ḥijāb*, refraining from performing prayer for the hypocrites, and taking the Maqam of Ibrahim as a place of prayer (2:125).

---

## Ayat 65–66: arguing about what you do not know

**The argument that refutes itself.** Ibn Kathir renders the sense of ayah 65 as: 'How is it that you, Jews, claim that Ibrahim was a Jew, although he lived before Allah sent down the Tawrāh to Mūsā? How is it that you, Christians, claim that Ibrahim was Christian, although Christianity came after his time?' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the futility of their exercise already stood exposed: both these ways in religion appeared long afterwards and simply did not exist before that — so how could it be claimed that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) adhered to them? Hence the closing rebuke of ayah 65 — *"Have you then no sense?"* This is not an appeal to revelation. It is an appeal to basic reasoning.

**Ayah 66 turns the knife.** *"Verily, you are those who have disputed about that of which you have knowledge. Why do you then dispute concerning that of which you have no knowledge?"* Ibn Kathir explains that this ayah criticizes those who argue and dispute without knowledge. Had they disputed about their religions, which they had knowledge of, and about the Law legislated for them until Muhammad ﷺ was sent, it would have been better for them. Instead they disputed about what they had no knowledge of at all. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the sharpening: if arguing on the basis of *incomplete* knowledge was already hollow, that they would venture to do so on the basis of *no* knowledge could hardly be explained.

**And where does knowledge belong?** Ibn Kathir says Allah commanded them to refer what they have no knowledge of to Him Who knows the seen and unseen matters and Who knows the true reality of all things — *"It is Allah Who knows, and you know not."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it simply: the truth is that only Allah knows the way of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). This ayah is a permanent rebuke to confident speech about religion without knowledge.

---

## Ayah 67: what Ibrahim actually was

*"Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a true Muslim, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the Mushrikīn."*

Having said what he was **not**, the ayah says what he **was**.
