Ibn Kathir glosses **ḥanīfan musliman** as "shunning Shirk and living in Imān" — a man who turned away from associating anything with Allah and lived in faith and submission to Him. *Mushrikīn* are those who associate partners with Allah, the very thing ayah 64 called all sides to renounce.

Ibn Kathir links this ayah to the ayah in Sūrat Al-Baqarah: *"And they say: Be Jews or Christians, then you will be guided"* (2:135) — the same demand to convert to a *label*, met with the same answer: Ibrahim's way came before all your labels.

---

## Ayah 68: who has the best claim to him

*"Verily, among mankind who have the best claim to Ibrahim are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who have believed. And Allah is the Walī (Protector and Helper) of the believers."*

The ayah settles the dispute not by counting genealogies but by naming a criterion: **following**. Ibn Kathir explains it as "the people who have the most right to be followers of Ibrahim are those who followed his religion and this Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ, and his Companions from the Muhājirīn, Anṣār and those who followed their lead." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way: the closest of people to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) were those who followed him during his time, and now the closest to him is the Prophet of Islam, Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, and so are the believers in him and in the past prophets.

Notice the phrase **"and this Prophet"** — in the middle of a debate about a patriarch who lived long ago, the claim is planted in the present, and Ibn Kathir identifies him plainly as Muhammad ﷺ.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that Saʿid bin Manṣur recorded that Ibn Masʿūd said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Every Prophet had a Walī (supporter, best friend) from among the Prophets. My Walī among them is my father Ibrahim, the Khalīl (intimate friend) of my Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored."

The Prophet ﷺ then recited this very ayah. The bond he claims with Ibrahim is not blood — it is that of a *walī*, a supporter and best friend, which is the same criterion the ayah itself lays down.

**"And Allah is the Walī of the believers."** Ibn Kathir explains: Allah is the Protector of all those who believe in His Messengers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that these believers are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, their guardian is Allah, and He will reward them for their belief. The ayah ends by turning the word *walī* back on Allah Himself: the moment you truly follow, you find that Allah is your Protector and Helper.

---

## Living it

**Lead with the common ground, but do not sell the message short.** Ayah 64 is the model: find the one thing your listener already affirms, name it honestly and fairly, and build the invitation on it — while stating your own position without ambiguity.

**Know when to stop.** *"Bear witness that we are Muslims"* is a complete and dignified ending. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's counsel is that once the truth has been proved clearly and still rejected, re-state what you believe and conclude the conversation rather than descend into altercation.

**Do not argue about what you do not know.** Ayah 66 does not censure disagreement as such; it censures speaking with confidence beyond your knowledge. "It is Allah Who knows, and you know not" is a sentence a believer should be able to say out loud without embarrassment.

**Audit your own obediences.** Ibn Jurayj's reading of "none of us shall take others as lords besides Allah" — "we do not obey each other in disobedience to Allah" — is the most searching line in the passage. Every time we follow a person or a crowd into what Allah has forbidden, we have edged toward the very thing this ayah asks all of us to renounce together.

**Claims are settled by following, not by naming.** Ayah 68 removes inherited identity as a basis for standing before Allah. The question is never which name you carry, but whose path you are actually walking.

passages.title: Attempts to mislead and the morning-evening ruse
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These six ayat expose a deliberate, organised attempt to pull Muslims away from their faith — and then dismantle it. What binds them into one unit is that the same actors run through all of them ("a party of the People of the Book"), pursuing the same aim (to mislead the believers), driven by the same motive that Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both name (envy), and receiving the same answer from Allah: guidance is His to give, and bounty is His to distribute.

The passage moves in three steps. First the desire is named (ayah 69). Then the accusations are laid out — you disbelieve against your own testimony, you blend truth with falsehood and bury what you know (ayat 70–71). Then the actual scheme is quoted in their own words, along with the internal policy that went with it (ayat 72–73), and answered with two "Say" statements that lift the whole matter out of human hands and place it in Allah's (ayat 73–74).

## "A party" — the Qur'an's precision

Ayah 69 opens with *waddat ṭā'ifatun min ahl al-kitāb* — "**Some** of the People of the Book wish to mislead you." Ayah 72 uses the same word again: "**A group** among the People of the Book said…" The Qur'an is not describing a whole people; it is describing a faction within them who took a decision and acted on it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: "**Some from among** the people of the Book chose a strategy of deception in order to mislead Muslims." Ibn Kathir's discussion identifies these plotters as Jews of that time, and the report he cites from Mujahid says the ayah "refers to the Jews." But the Qur'an's own word choice keeps the charge exactly where it belongs — on the party that plotted, not on everyone who carried a scripture.

Notice, too, what the ayah names first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says verse 69 "exposes the cherished desire of the people of the Book to mislead Muslims away from the true faith they are on." Before there was a plot, there was a longing. The scheme quoted in ayah 72 is that longing worked out into a plan.

## The boomerang in ayah 69

"But they shall not lead astray anyone except themselves, and they perceive not."

Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: the punishment of this behaviour falls back upon them, while they remain unaware. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the text "firmly declares that the victim of their effort to misguide is no one other than themselves, something they do not realize."

Two things are worth sitting with here. The first is the reversal itself: an effort aimed outward lands inward. The second is the closing phrase — "they perceive not." Both sources stress this unawareness: they do not realise it. The scheme feels workable to the schemers the entire time it is costing them. They are not told they will one day be caught; they are told they are already the casualty, and that they cannot feel it.

## Two charges, ayat 70–71

**Ayah 70: disbelief against your own testimony.** "O People of the Book! Why do you reject the signs of Allah while you bear witness?" Ibn Kathir's comment is short and pointed: "You know for certain that Allah's Ayat are true and authentic." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies which signs are meant — "the verses in Torah and Injil which prove the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ" — and draws out the logic: to deny his prophethood "amounts to declaring these verses to be false which is infidelity, although they themselves confirm these as true." They are caught between two claims that cannot both stand. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this "an admonition on their error in belief."

**Ayah 71: mixing and concealing.** "Why do you mix the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?" These are two distinct operations. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the mixing as confusing "the real statement, that is, the prophecy about the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ with the fictitious, that is, the interpolated statements or false exegesis" — that is, material inserted into the text, or a reading forced onto it. Ibn Kathir explains the concealing as "hiding what is in your Books about the description of Muhammad ﷺ, while you know what you do."

Mixing and hiding are the two ways truth gets buried. You can bury it under silence, or you can bury it under added material until no one can find it. Both are named here, and both, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses, were done "despite knowing the truth, and knowing that they are hiding it."

**A careful qualification from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.** The phrases "while you bear witness" (70) and "while you know" (71) might be misread as implying that disbelief would somehow be acceptable from someone who did not testify or did not know. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān blocks that reading directly: these words "should not be taken to mean that disbelief will become permissible for them if they do not attest to the truth or have no knowledge about it. This is because kufr (disbelief) is intrinsically an abominable thing to practice. This is prohibited under all conditions." The mention of knowledge and testimony is not a condition on the ruling; it is there, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, "to increase the impact of reproachment." Knowing makes the sin uglier; not knowing would not have made it fine.

## The morning-evening ruse, ayah 72

Now the Qur'an quotes them. They said to one another: "Believe in the morning in that which is revealed to the believers, and reject it at the end of the day, so that they may turn back."

Ibn Kathir describes the mechanics. This was "a wicked plan from the People of the Book to deceive Muslims who are weak in the religion." They would pretend to be believers at the beginning of the day — specifically, Ibn Kathir says, "by attending the dawn prayer with the Muslims." Then, when the day ended, they would revert to their old religion, so that ignorant people would say: "They reverted to their old religion because they uncovered some shortcomings in the Islamic religion."

Ibn Kathir supports this with a report: Ibn Abi Najih said that Mujahid commented about this ayah, which refers to the Jews — "They attended the dawn prayer with the Prophet ﷺ and disbelieved in the end of the day in order to misguide the people. This way, people would think that they have uncovered shortcomings in the religion that they briefly followed." (This is the comment of Mujahid, as Ibn Kathir transmits it — an exegetical remark, not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads their calculation the same way and adds the psychology: they expected the "quick about-turn" to "create doubts in the minds of Muslims about Qur'an and Islam," so that Muslims might turn away from their faith "thinking that there must be something wrong with Islam visible to such learned people who were open-minded enough to accept it first."

That last line names the hinge of the scheme. What was meant to do the work was not an argument but the standing of the men making the exit — they were, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "such learned people," and their withdrawal was expected to be read as a verdict. This is also why, on Ibn Kathir's account, the plot required them actually to pray fajr with the Muslims: the entry had to look genuine for the departure to carry weight.

## The internal policy, ayah 73

Their instruction to each other continues: "And only believe those who follow your religion."

Ibn Kathir explains this as an order about disclosure: "do not trust anyone with your secret knowledge, except those who follow your religion. Therefore, they say, do not expose your knowledge to Muslims in order to prevent them from believing in it and, thus, use it as proof against you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the double standard in a single line: "Sincerity with the later, expediency with the former!" — their true belief affirmed "before none but only those who follow their own creed," while the declaration made in front of Muslims was, in its words, "feinted."

The rest of what they said makes the fear explicit: "Do not believe that anyone can receive like that which you have received, otherwise they would engage you in argument before your Lord." Ibn Kathir unpacks it: "Do not disclose the knowledge that you have to the Muslims, to prevent them from learning it and thus becoming your equals. They will be even better because they will believe in it or will use it against you as evidence with your Lord, and thus establish Allah's proof against you in this life and the Hereafter."

Read that carefully. It is a confession. Their own reasoning takes for granted that the knowledge they hold is true, that Muslims would believe it if they saw it, and that it could be used against the concealers before their Lord. Nobody builds a blackout around a text he thinks is worthless.

## The two answers: "Say…"

Against all this scheming, Allah instructs the Prophet ﷺ to say two things.

**"Verily, right guidance is the guidance of Allah."** Ibn Kathir: Allah guides the hearts of the faithful "to the perfect faith through the clear Ayat, plain proofs and unequivocal evidence that He has sent down to His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ" — and this occurs, he adds, addressing them directly, "even though you hide the description of Muhammad ﷺ. The unlettered Prophet whom you find in your Books that you received from the earlier Prophets." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion: their clever moves are not going to work for them, "since Guidance given to servants of Allah is certainly from Allah. So, it is He who, with Guidance in His control, can make whoever He will steadfast on that Guidance. No one can succeed in weaning such a person away from it with any trick, plan or enticement whatsoever."

The entire plot assumed that faith is a social product — that it can be manufactured or dismantled by managing what people see other people do. The answer, as both sources give it, places guidance in Allah's control: it is not yours to manufacture, and it is not yours to dismantle.

**"All the bounty is in the Hand of Allah; He grants to whom He wills."** Ibn Kathir draws out what the statement establishes: "meaning, all affairs are under His control, and He gives and takes. Verily, Allah gives faith, knowledge and sound comprehension to whomever He wills. He also misguides whomever He wills… Allah has the perfect wisdom and the unequivocal proofs."

The ayah then closes with two of Allah's names, *Wāsiʿ* and *ʿAlīm*, rendered in the source as "All-Sufficient for His creatures' needs, All-Knower." The plot ran on holding things back — guard the knowledge, keep it from the Muslims. The ayah answers with a giving that is not in their custody at all: He grants to whom He wills, and He is the One who gives faith, knowledge and sound comprehension to whomever He wills.

## Ayah 74: the root cause, and its cure

"He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy. And Allah is the Owner of great bounty."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the motive that has been running underneath the whole passage: **envy**. "The reason why they act in the way they do is envy, that is, they envy Muslims as to why they were given the Scripture, or they envy their supremacy in religious argument. It is because of this envy that they keep working to bring about the downfall of Islam and of the community that adheres to it." Ibn Kathir heads his discussion of these ayat in the same terms — the envy felt towards the Muslims and the plots that came out of it.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies why ayah 74 is the cure rather than merely the conclusion: this envy "is based on not knowing the nature, timing and wisdom of Allah's grace and mercy," which is what "the later part of verse 73 and… verse 74" set out. Envy, on that reading, is a failure to understand how Allah assigns His gifts. *Yakhtaṣṣu bi-raḥmatihi man yashā'* — "He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy" — addresses exactly that ignorance: the choosing is His, and His wisdom governs it.

Ibn Kathir ends by turning the ayah toward the believers: Allah "has endowed you, O believers, with tremendous virtue, in that He honored your Prophet Muhammad ﷺ over all other prophets, and by directing you to the best Shari'ah there is." The passage that began by describing people consumed by what someone else received closes by telling the recipients what they have.

## Living it

**Faith is not decided by who walks away from it.** The plot in ayah 72 worked entirely on the expectation that Muslims would read a respected person's exit as a verdict on the religion — that they would conclude, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "that there must be something wrong with Islam." Ayah 73 answers that guidance is from Allah, given through "the clear Ayat, plain proofs and unequivocal evidence." When someone knowledgeable or admired publicly abandons the religion, that event carries no argument inside it. Ask what the evidence is; do not read the exit as the evidence.

**Concealed knowledge testifies against the one who conceals it.** Ayah 71 condemns burying the truth and blending it with falsehood, and ayah 73 records the plotters' own fear that what they hid would "establish Allah's proof against you in this life and the Hereafter." Anyone who holds knowledge that would help people, and withholds it to protect his position, should read their words in ayah 73 with a shiver.

**Guard against the double standard.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's line — "Sincerity with the later, expediency with the former!" — describes a habit that is not confined to one community. Faith that is performed for one audience and disowned before another is exactly what ayah 72 puts on record.

**Treat envy as a failure of understanding, not just a bad feeling.** Ayah 74 does not tell the envious to feel better. It tells them who assigns mercy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the envy in this passage to "not knowing the nature, timing and wisdom of Allah's grace and mercy." The remedy it points to is therefore not suppression of the feeling but knowledge of Whose choosing it is: "He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy. And Allah is the Owner of great bounty."

passages.title: Trusts honoured and covenants sold cheaply
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take a very ordinary thing — money you lend someone and whether they give it back — and show that it is never only about money. A debt honoured or dodged is a covenant kept or sold. Ayah 75 draws the portrait of two kinds of people among the People of the Book, and exposes the religious excuse the dishonest ones used; ayah 76 answers that excuse with the principle that saves a person; ayah 77 states the terrible price of trading the covenant of Allah for a small gain. Fairness, honesty and dread of the Last Day hold the passage together as one argument.

## Where this falls in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the thread. In the preceding ayat (70–72) the sūrah exposed a breach of faith by some of the People of the Book: disbelieving in the verses of Allah, confusing truth with falsehood, concealing the truth, and conspiring to mislead the believers. Now, in ayah 75, the same breach of faith is traced into a much more everyday arena — property and trust. And because some among them genuinely were trustworthy, both types are identified rather than everyone being tarred with one brush.

## Two kinds of people (ayah 75)

The ayah sets up a deliberate contrast. Among them is one who, if you entrust him with a *qinṭār* — Ibn Kathir glosses this as a great amount of wealth — will readily pay it back. And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a single coin, will not repay it "unless you constantly stand demanding," insisting on getting your rightful property.

Ibn Kathir draws out the logic on both sides. The man who returns a fortune would obviously give back what is less than a fortune; that is plain. And the man who will not release a single dinar unless you stand over him — what do you imagine he does with more than a dinar? The Qur'an picks the extreme in each direction, so that everything in between is settled by implication. One sentence, and you have a complete map of human character in matters of trust.

**Why this matters:** the ayah does not say "the People of the Book are dishonest." It says *among* them is this, and *among* them is that. The dishonesty is real and named, but so is the honesty.

## Praising good in someone outside the faith

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a question a careful reader will feel. If the praise in ayah 75 refers to those of the People of the Book who had embraced Islam, praising them poses no problem. But if it refers to the People of the Book in the absolute sense, including those who did not believe, then a question arises: when no act of a disbeliever is acceptable, why praise them at all?

The answer given is precise: for a deed to become *acceptable* is one matter, and having a word of praise for it is something else. From praising something it does not follow that it is acceptable with Allah. The purpose is to point out that something good, even the good of a disbeliever, is good to a certain degree — the benefit of which he receives in this mortal world in the form of a good reputation, and in the Hereafter in the form of a reduction in the punishment for his disbelief.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then makes the wider observation: this makes clear that Islam does not resort to prejudice and short-sightedness. On the contrary, it shows open-hearted appreciation of the excellence of even its adversary. That is a demanding standard for anyone who argues about religion online.

## The excuse — and why it was a lie

The ayah then reports the reasoning behind the betrayal: "There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered ones." Ibn Kathir explains what made them reject what they owed: they said, "There is no harm in our religion if we eat up the property of the unlettered ones, the Arabs, for Allah has allowed it for us."

Notice the shape of this. It is not simple greed; greed does not need a doctrine. This is theft dressed as theology — a rule invented to make the victim's property lawful because of who the victim was. That is exactly why the ayah closes as it does: **"but they tell a lie against Allah while they know it."** Ibn Kathir is blunt: they invented this lie and word of misguidance; rather, Allah would not have allowed that money for them unless they had a right to it. The words "while they know it" are the sharpest part — this was not an honest mistake in reasoning. They knew.

## Ibn ʿAbbās turns the mirror around

The most striking thing in Ibn Kathir's treatment of ayah 75 is that he does not leave this as a criticism of somebody else. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded that Ṣaʿṣaʿah bin Yazīd said that a man asked Ibn ʿAbbās: "During battle, we capture some property belonging to *Ahl Adh-Dhimmah* — the non-Muslims living under the protection of the Muslim state — such as chickens and sheep." Ibn ʿAbbās said, "What do you do in this case?" The man said, "We say that there is no sin in it."

Ibn ʿAbbās answered: **that is what the People of the Book said** — "There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered ones." And he added: if they pay the jizyah — the tax due from non-Muslim citizens living under Muslim rule — then you are not allowed their property, except when they willingly give it up.

Read that again. A Muslim, using a Muslim's version of the same excuse, is told by Ibn ʿAbbās that he has landed in the very verse he thought was about other people. The passage is a mirror, not a weapon.

## The lender may keep asking (a legal point from ayah 75)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a ruling derived from the very phrase "unless you keep standing over him." From this, Imām Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) deduced that the lender has the right to keep pursuing the borrower until he receives his due — a point reported via Qurṭubī. The Qur'an describes the creditor standing over the debtor as a fact of the situation; the jurist reads in it a right that is not taken away.

## "Yes" — the answer in ayah 76

Ayah 76 opens with a single word of rebuttal: *balā*, rendered "Yes" and "Absolutely!" The claim was: *we are under no obligation toward these people.* The answer is: **yes there is — whoever fulfils his pledge and fears Allah much, then indeed Allah loves the muttaqīn, the pious.**

Two things are worth slowing down for here.

**First, the word ʿahd.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes it sharply from *waʿdah*. An *ʿahd* — a pledge or covenant — is what gets settled between the parties concerned after mutual discussion, and by which both of them have to abide. A *waʿdah*, a promise, issues forth from a single side. In short: an ʿahd is bilateral, a waʿdah unilateral. That is why breaking an ʿahd is so grave: there is another party standing on the other end of it, waiting.

**Second, the covenant Ibn Kathir has in view.** He reads the address as directed to the People of the Book: whoever among you fulfils his promise and fears Allah regarding the covenant Allah took from you — that you would believe in Muhammad ﷺ when he is sent, just as He took the same covenant from all the Prophets and their nations — and whoever avoids Allah's prohibitions, obeys Him, and adheres to the Sharīʿah He sent with His final Messenger ﷺ. So the covenant over a coin and the covenant over the Messenger are being spoken of in one breath. A man's handling of a debt and his handling of revelation come out of the same character.

**And then: "Allah loves the muttaqīn."** After all the exposure of betrayal, the ayah ends not with a threat but with love. Note also who is loved: not a tribe, not a lineage — *whoever* fulfils his pledge and fears Allah. The door in ayah 76 is deliberately left open to anyone.

## The transaction that ruins a man (ayah 77)

Ayah 77 casts the sin as a purchase: those who **purchase a small gain at the cost of Allah's covenant and their oaths.** They are traders — and the ayah's contempt is in the pricing. Ibn Kathir explains it as preferring the small things of this short, soon-to-end life over fulfilling what they had promised Allah: to follow Muhammad ﷺ, to announce his description from their books to people, and to affirm his truth.

Then comes the sentence, and Ibn Kathir takes it clause by clause:

- **"They shall have no portion in the Hereafter"** — they will not have a share or part in the Hereafter's rewards.
- **"Neither will Allah speak to them"** — He will not speak words of kindness to them.
- **"Nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection"** — He will not look at them with any mercy.
- **"Nor will He purify them"** — from sins and impurities; rather, He will order them to the Fire.
- **"And they shall have a painful torment."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts these as five warnings given to those who break their solemn pledge. On the first — that they will have no share in the blessings of heaven — it cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that one who usurps the right of a Muslim under a false oath makes the Fire of Hell compulsory for himself. The narrator asked whether that holds even for something very insignificant. He answered: even if it be the green bough of a tree. (Muslim, via Mazharī.)

On the fourth warning it adds a hard note: Allah will not forgive them their sins, since they wasted away the rights of a servant of Allah through breach of trust, and Allah will not forgive what one human being owes to another human being. In Islamic terminology this is known as *ḥaqq al-ʿabd*, the right of a servant of Allah.

## The man who gave up his land

Ibn Kathir gives us both the occasion of revelation and, alongside it, one of the most beautiful scenes in the tafsīr of this sūrah.

**The occasion.** Al-Ashʿath said: "By Allah! This verse was revealed concerning me." He owned some land with a Jewish man who denied his right, and he complained against him to the Messenger of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ asked him, "Do you have evidence?" He said, "I don't have evidence." So the Prophet ﷺ said to the other man, "Take an oath then." Al-Ashʿath said: "O Allah's Messenger! He will take a false oath immediately, and I will lose my property." Then Allah revealed *"Verily, those who purchase a small gain at the cost of Allah's covenant and their oaths…"* Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded this hadith.

Look at what the ayah is doing. The court runs on evidence, and where there is no evidence the oath stands — which means a shameless man can win a case. Ayah 77 does not overturn the procedure. It tells the man who wins that way exactly what he has bought, and with whose money he will pay for it.

**The scene.** Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAdī bin ʿAmīrah al-Kindī said that Imru' al-Qays bin ʿĀbis, a man from Kindah, disputed with a man from Ḥaḍramawt before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning a piece of land. The Prophet ﷺ required the man from Ḥaḍramawt to present his evidence, but he did not have any. So the Prophet ﷺ required Imru' al-Qays to swear to his truthfulness. The man from Ḥaḍramawt said, "O Messenger of Allah! If you only require him to swear, then by the Lord of the Kaʿbah, my land is lost." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Whoever swears while lying to acquire the property of others will meet Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while He is angry with him."** Rajāʼ, one of the narrators, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ then recited this ayah.

Then Imru' al-Qays said, "What if one forfeits this dispute, what will he gain, O Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet ﷺ answered: **"Paradise."** Imru' al-Qays said: "Bear witness that I forfeit all the land for him." (An-Nasāʼī also recorded this hadith.)

He was one oath away from winning. He heard the price, and he walked away from the land.

## Others who will not be spoken to or looked at

Ibn Kathir gathers further ahadith under this ayah, because the same threefold punishment appears in the Sunnah attached to several sins:

- Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Dharr said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said there are three persons whom Allah will not speak to, nor look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify, and they shall taste a painful torment. Abū Dharr said, "O Messenger of Allah! Who are they, may they gain failure and loss?" Repeating the statement three times, he said: the *musbil* (the man whose clothes reach below the ankles), he who swears while lying so as to sell his merchandise, and the one who gives charity and then reminds people of it. Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan.
- Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAbdullāh said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever takes a false oath to deprive a Muslim of his property will meet Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while He is angry with him.
- Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ named three of the same description: a man who does not give the wayfarer some of the surplus water that he has; a man who swears, while lying, in order to complete a sales transaction after the ʿAṣr prayer; and a man who gives his pledge of allegiance to a leader, fulfilling the pledge if he is given something and breaking it if he is not. Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī also recorded it, and At-Tirmidhī graded it Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ.

The common thread is unmistakable: **using the name of Allah as an instrument to take what is not yours.** The oath is meant to be the last resort of truth; these people turned it into a tool of theft.

## Living it

The passage is severe, but its demand is simple.

**Return what you are trusted with — the small even more carefully than the large.** Ayah 75 makes the single coin the test, not the *qinṭār*. Most people are honest about large sums, where the stakes are visible; character shows in the borrowed small thing that nobody is chasing you for.

**Refuse the exemption clause.** The sin condemned in ayah 75 is not merely taking; it is constructing a reason why *these particular people* do not have to be paid — because they are outsiders, ignorant, an institution, a foreigner, a faceless company. Ibn ʿAbbās applied that verdict to Muslims doing the same thing. Any reasoning that ends in "so it isn't really wrong in their case" deserves the suspicion of ayah 75.

**Never use Allah's name to close a deal.** Ayah 77 prices the false oath: no portion in the Hereafter, no kind word, no merciful glance, no purification, and a painful torment — for a gain the Qur'an itself calls small. And the hadith cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves no room to plead that the amount was trivial: even if it be the green bough of a tree.

**And weigh what is owed to people, not only what is owed to Allah.** The fourth warning is the one to sit with: Allah will not forgive what one human being owes to another human being — *ḥaqq al-ʿabd*, the right of a servant of Allah.

**Be the first man in ayah 75.** Be the one who, when trusted with a fortune, hands it back — so that the smaller things need no discussion at all. Ayah 76 tells you what that earns: not a reputation, but the love of Allah.

passages.title: Twisting Scripture, and the prophet who never claimed worship
passages.tafsir:
# Āl ʿImrān 78–80: Twisting Scripture, and the prophet who never claimed worship

These three ayat expose two related frauds and demolish both. Ayah 78 exposes people who bend the sacred text with their tongues so that their own words sound like revelation; ayat 79–80 then close off the deepest form of that fraud — the claim that a prophet ever invited people to worship him, or any angel or prophet, alongside Allah. What holds the passage together is a single thread: **words falsely placed in Allah's mouth, and worship falsely placed at a creature's feet.**

## The moment behind the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the occasion. It was during the presence of the deputation from Najrān that some Jews and Christians said to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Muhammad, do you want us to worship you the way Christians worship Jesus, son of Mary?" He answered: "I seek refuge with Allah that we worship someone other than Allah or call on others to do so. Allah Almighty has not sent us to do that." Thereupon, Maʿārif reports, this verse was revealed.

(This is the report as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits it; the bundle names no hadith collection for the Prophet's ﷺ words, so they are conveyed here exactly as the commentary gives them, with no collection attached.)

Notice what that sequence does to the shape of the passage. A question was put to him about being worshipped; he refused it and disclaimed any such mission; and then revelation came down — not merely to confirm his answer, but to state it as a rule about prophethood as such. Ibn Kathir titles his comment on ayat 79–80 in exactly those terms: **no prophet ever called people to worship him, or to worship other than Allah.**

## Ayah 78 — "they distort the Book with their tongues"

**A party, not a people.** The wording is precise: *wa inna minhum la-farīqan* — "and verily, among them is a party." Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps that limit in place, and he speaks of "some Jews" rather than all. The charge is aimed at a faction, not flung at everyone.

**The twisting happens in the tongue.** In the Arabic phrase Ibn Kathir comments on — *yalwūna alsinatahum bil-kitāb* — the object of the bending verb is not the Book but *alsinatahum*, their tongues. What is bent is the delivery, "so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book." Then comes the second, bolder step in the same ayah: "and they say: This is from Allah, but it is not from Allah." First the appearance, then the claim.

Ibn Kathir explains that they "distort Allah's Words with their tongues, change them from their appropriate places, and alter their intended meanings," and that the aim is **to deceive the ignorant people** — making it appear that their own words are in the Book of Allah. The early authorities he cites — Mujāhid, ash-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas — gloss the phrase simply and devastatingly: "They alter them."

**They knew.** The ayah does not end with the lie; it ends with *wa hum yaʿlamūn* — "while they know it." Ibn Kathir stresses that they attribute their own lies to Allah "even though they know that they have lied and invented falsehood." That final clause is what marks this out as a deliberate lie rather than an honest mistake.

## What exactly was altered? A real difference among the scholars

Ibn Kathir preserves an important discussion here, and it is worth following carefully because the commentators do not all say the same thing.

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**, in a report Ibn Kathir attributes to **al-Bukhārī**, held that the ayah means they *alter and add*, while none among Allah's creation can remove the Words of Allah from His Books — what they alter and distort is the apparent meaning.
- **Wahb bin Munabbih**, in a statement Ibn Kathir says **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** recorded, went further in the same direction: "The Tawrāh and the Injīl remain as Allah revealed them, and no letter in them was removed. However, the people misguide others by addition and false interpretation, relying on books that they wrote themselves." As for Allah's Books, he concluded, "they are still preserved and cannot be changed."
- **Ibn Kathir himself** then draws a distinction rather than simply agreeing. If Wahb meant the books currently in the hands of the People of the Book, Ibn Kathir says there is no doubt that they altered, distorted, added to and deleted from them — he points in particular to the Arabic versions of these books, which in his words contain tremendous error, many additions and deletions, and enormous misinterpretation by translators whose comprehension he judges incorrect. But if Wahb meant the Books of Allah that He has with Him, then "these Books are preserved and were never changed."

That distinction is the useful takeaway: **revelation as it is with Allah is untouchable; revelation as it passes through human hands, tongues and translations is exactly where the tampering happens.** The ayah is describing an assault on transmission and meaning.

## Ayah 79 — the sentence a prophet cannot utter

The ayah opens with *mā kāna li-basharin* — a construction the sources render two ways that illuminate each other. The translation in front of you has "it is not appropriate"; Ibn Kathir's rendering has "it is not (possible)." Both senses are being carried: it is unbecoming, and it is not going to happen.

Three gifts are named as the setting — **the Book, al-Ḥukm, and prophethood**. Ibn Kathir glosses that middle term as knowledge in the Law; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering speaks of the Book, the Wisdom and the power of making decisions, together with the great station of prophethood. These are precisely the credentials that would make such a claim persuasive if it were ever made — and Ibn Kathir's whole point is that it never was.

Ibn Kathir draws the argument out to its logical edge: for such a person to proclaim "Worship me instead of Allah" — which he explains means *along with* Allah — is not the right of a Prophet or a Messenger, "then indeed, it is not the right of anyone else to issue such a claim." **If the highest human station cannot claim worship, no lower station can.**

The criticism, he says, refers to the ignorant rabbis, priests and teachers of misguidance — unlike the Messengers and their sincere, knowledgeable followers who implement their knowledge, who command only what Allah commands them and forbid only what Allah forbade, as their honourable Messengers conveyed to them. He describes the Messengers as "the emissaries between Allah and His creation, conveying Allah's Message and Trust" — and they fulfilled that mission, gave sincere advice to creation, and conveyed the truth to them.

## "Be Rabbāniyyūn" — what a prophet says instead

The ayah does not merely deny; it supplies the alternative: *"On the contrary (he would say): Be you Rabbāniyyūn, because you are teaching the Book, and you are studying it."* Ibn Kathir notes that this means the Messenger *recommends* the people to be Rabbāniyyūn.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Razīn and several others explained **Rabbāniyyūn** as meaning "wise, learned, and forbearing." So the prophetic ambition for a community is not a crowd of devotees gathered around a personality; it is a people made wise, learned and forbearing.

And the ayah grounds that in two ongoing activities: **teaching the Book** and **studying it**. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk's comment on that phrase is striking: "Whoever learns the Qurʼān deserves to become a Faqīh (learned)." On the second phrase, *wa bimā kuntum tadrusūn*, Ibn Kathir adds a short gloss: **preserving its words.**

Read that against ayah 78 and the passage snaps into focus. The party in ayah 78 *alter* the words; the Rabbāniyyūn in ayah 79 are commended for *preserving* them. Both groups are occupied with scripture. The difference is what their handling does to the text.

## Ayah 80 — not even angels, not even prophets

Ayah 80 shuts the last door: *"Nor would he order you to take angels and Prophets for lords."* Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and needs no more: the Prophet does not command worshipping other than Allah, "whether a sent Messenger or an angel." The two highest categories of created excellence are named here — and if they are excluded, nothing below them can qualify.

Then the closing question: *"Would he order you to disbelieve after you have submitted to Allah's will?"* Ibn Kathir reads it as a denial — he would not do that — and gives the reason with startling directness: **"for whoever calls to worshipping other than Allah, will have called to Kufr."** The Prophets only call to īmān, which commands worshipping Allah alone without partners.

Ibn Kathir then lines up the Qurʼān's own witnesses that this is the universal pattern of prophethood:

- *"And We did not send any Messenger before you (O Muhammad ﷺ) but We revealed to him (saying): 'None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me.'"* (21:25)
- *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger (proclaiming): 'Worship Allah (Alone), and avoid Ṭāghūt (all false deities).'"* (16:36) — the bracketed gloss is the source's own, and it is the key to the word: *Ṭāghūt* here covers everything falsely set up as a deity.
- *"And ask those of Our Messengers whom We sent before you: 'Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Gracious (Allah)?'"* (43:45)

And concerning the angels, he cites: *"And if any of them should say: 'Verily, I am a god besides Him (Allah),' such a one We should recompense with Hell. Thus We recompense the wrongdoers."* (21:29). The very beings people are tempted to elevate are themselves addressed by that warning.

## The argument from Allah's knowledge

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds a distinct argument here, and it is worth following because it moves from theology to logic and back.

Any government of this world, it observes, weighs two things before appointing someone to an office of responsibility: does the person have the ability to comprehend and execute policy, and how far can he be expected to carry out directives and keep the subjects in a stable stance of loyalty? No king or parliament would ever appoint as its representative or ambassador someone about whom there exists the least doubt of anti-government activity or deviation from policy. The difference is that a worldly government may fail to assess a person's ability or loyalty correctly. With Allah, Maʿārif says, even that element of doubt does not exist. If Allah knows of a man that he would not overstep the bounds of loyalty and obedience even in the slightest degree, then it is impossible that he could later prove contrary to that assessment — "otherwise, it would mean that Divine knowledge is defective (we seek refuge with Allah!)".

Right from here, Maʿārif says, the question of **ʿiṣmah** becomes clear. The commentary's own footnote defines it: "a special protection given to someone by Allah which makes him refrain from sins," translated for brevity as *infallibility*. Its conclusion: now that the blessed prophets are free of minor sins, how could the probability of their committing shirk — associating others with Allah — or of revolting against Allah remain valid?

## Who exactly is being answered

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsīr ʿUsmānī, names three groups addressed by this passage, and uses a different verb for each:

1. **The Christians** — here, ʿUsmānī says, is "the necessary refutation of the Christians who claimed that it was Masīḥ (peace be upon him) who asked them to have belief in his sonship and godhead."
2. **The Muslims** who had gone to the Prophet ﷺ "trying to find out if it was all right for them to prostrate before him rather than greet him with the usual *salām*." They too, ʿUsmānī says, were chastised.
3. **The People of the Book** who "had invested their rabbis and monks with the station of God. Refuge with Allah!" — the very pattern ayah 80 forbids.

That second entry deserves a pause. The passage's rebuke is not aimed only outward at Christians and People of the Book; on ʿUsmānī's reading, Muslims are named among those chastised, and the matter at issue was a question about prostration put to the Prophet ﷺ himself.

## Living it

**Check the source, not the tone.** The party in ayah 78 succeeded through *delivery* — words made to sound as if they sat inside the Book. Ibn Kathir says plainly that the target was the ignorant. The defence is knowing where a claim actually comes from before letting it into your religion, and being unimpressed by a reverent tone that carries no source.

**Never say "this is from Allah" loosely.** The ayah's severity falls on those who attach Allah's name to what Allah did not say — knowingly. That should make anyone slow to declare "Islam says…" about matters they have not verified.

**Aim at Rabbāniyyah.** The alternative the ayah puts in place of misplaced devotion is to become wise, learned and forbearing through teaching and studying the Book — and, in Ibn Kathir's gloss, preserving its words. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk's line sets the bar within reach: whoever learns the Qurʼān deserves to become learned in it.

**The boundary runs inside the community too.** Ayah 80's line — not angels, not prophets — is not coldness toward the righteous; Ibn Kathir is careful to exempt the Messengers and their sincere, knowledgeable followers from the criticism. But ʿUsmānī's list is a reminder that the warning was heard by Muslims as well, over a question that arose within reach of the Prophet ﷺ. What belongs to Allah alone is guarded most carefully exactly where reverence runs highest.

passages.title: The prophets' covenant and no religion but submission
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Before any prophet ever stood before his people, Allah bound them all by a solemn pledge: whatever Book and wisdom I give you, when a Messenger comes after you confirming what you already have, you must believe in him and support him. Ayat 81–85 unfold from that one scene. If every prophet was bound by it, then whoever turns away after this is among the rebellious (ayah 82); then it is a rebuke to go seeking some religion other than Allah's when all creation already submits to Him (ayah 83); then the confession is the one dictated in ayah 84 — we believe in all of them without picking and choosing; and then the conclusion in ayah 85: whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.

The thread holding the five ayat together is this: revelation is one continuous covenant, and *Islam* is simply the name for keeping it.

## The covenant taken from the prophets (81)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah took this pledge **from every Prophet He sent, from Adam until ʿĪsā**. The condition is stated first: *"Take whatever I gave you from the Book and Ḥikmah"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, *if I give you the Book and the Ḥikmah*. (*Ḥikmah* is rendered "the Wisdom" in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, which pairs it with "the power of making decisions.") Then comes the obligation: *"and afterwards there will come to you a Messenger confirming what is with you; you must, then, believe in him and help him."*

Notice what this dismantles. Ibn Kathir's wording is careful: the prophets received the Book and the Ḥikmah, *"thus acquiring whatever high grades they deserve"* — and yet, *"even though Allah has given the Prophets the knowledge and the prophethood, this fact should not make them refrain from following and supporting the Prophet who comes after them."* Rank does not exempt anyone from the truth. If the prophets themselves were bound to receive a later Messenger, no one who comes after them can claim that what he already holds excuses him from what arrives next.

## "Isrī" — the weight of a single word

Allah then asks them directly: *"Do you agree (to it) and will you take up Isrī?"* This is the hinge of the ayah, and the early authorities gave it careful attention.

**Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ, Qatādah and as-Suddī** all said *Isrī* means **"My covenant."** **Muhammad bin Isḥāq** put it differently, saying it means *"the responsibility of My covenant that you took"* — that is, as the passage glosses it, **the ratified pledge that you gave Me**.

The two readings sit together, but Ibn Isḥāq's wording places the accent on *responsibility*: not merely the agreement, but what the one agreeing has taken on his shoulders.

Their answer is a single word: *"We agree."* And then the seal: *"Then bear witness; and I am with you among the witnesses."* The prophets are called to bear witness to the pledge, and Allah declares Himself among the witnesses to it.

## Ayah 82: "then whoever turns away"

Ayah 82 is the covenant's sanction, and Ibn Kathir ties it directly to what precedes: *"then whoever turns away after this"* — meaning, in his words, **from fulfilling this pledge and covenant** — *"they are the rebellious."*

The Arabic word rendered "the rebellious" here is *al-fāsiqūn*. The severity comes from the setting. The turning away in question is not that of someone who was never addressed; it follows immediately upon *aqrarnā* — "we agree."

## Two readings of the covenant, and why both stand

Who exactly was bound, and to whom?

**ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib and his cousin ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās** said: *"Allah never sent a Prophet but after taking his pledge that if Muhammad ﷺ were sent in his lifetime, he would believe in and support him."* And Allah commanded each prophet to take a pledge from his own nation that if Muhammad ﷺ were sent in their time, they would believe in and support him.

**Ṭāwūs, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah** read it more broadly: *"Allah took the pledge from the Prophets that they would believe in each other."*

Ibn Kathir does not set these against each other. He notes plainly that the second statement **"does not contradict what ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās stated."** The general principle — that the prophets were pledged to believe in one another — and the specific application to the final Messenger sit comfortably together.

## The rank this establishes for the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion out at length. Because that pledge was taken, **Muhammad ﷺ is the Final Prophet until the Day of Resurrection**. He is, in Ibn Kathir's words, *the greatest Imām, who if he existed in any time period, deserves to be obeyed, rather than all other Prophets.*

He then mentions three things that follow from this:

- **The night of Isrāʾ.** This, says Ibn Kathir, is why the Prophet ﷺ **led the prophets in prayer** when they gathered at Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).
- **The intercession on the Day of Gathering**, when the Lord comes to judge between His servants.
- **Al-Maqām al-Maḥmūd**, the praised station (Ibn Kathir refers the reader to 17:79), which *"only Muhammad deserves, a responsibility which the mighty Prophets and Messengers will decline to assume"* — while Muhammad ﷺ will carry the task of intercession.

That last line is worth sitting with. The station is described not as a privilege others were denied, but as a weight others will decline. He carries what no one else would carry.

## What a prophet can never do — the point Maʿārif ul Qurʾān presses

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān takes the ayah in a complementary direction. If Allah entrusts a man with the Book, the Wisdom, and the power of making decisions, and places him *"on the great station of prophethood,"* then he is always faithful to his mission: he calls people to become the faithful servants of Allah. That he would instead *"start moving people away from the worship of only one"* Lord and begin asking them to worship him, or to worship some other creature, **is something he can never do**. Were that possible, it would mean the one Allah sent as His messenger *"did not, in fact, deserve this designation."*

The tafsir makes this vivid with a comparison from ordinary life. Any government appointing someone to an office of responsibility weighs two things: can he comprehend and execute policy, and how far can he be expected to carry out directives and hold people in a stable stance of loyalty? No king or parliament would appoint as its representative or ambassador a man about whom there exists the least doubt of disloyalty. But a government *can* fail to assess a man's ability or loyalty correctly. **With Allah even that element of doubt does not exist.** If Allah knows of a man that he will not overstep the bounds of loyalty and obedience even in the slightest degree, it is impossible that he should later prove contrary to that — *"otherwise, it would mean that Divine knowledge is defective (we seek refuge with Allah!)."*

From here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, the question of **ʿiṣmah** becomes clear. The commentary's own editorial footnote defines the term: *"ʿIṣmah means a special protection given to someone by Allah which makes him refrain from sins,"* translated for brevity as "infallibility." And it presses the argument: now that the blessed prophets are free of minor sins, how can the probability remain of their committing **shirk** — which the commentary glosses as "the major sin of associating others with Allah" — or of revolting against Allah?

The tafsir then names three targets of this correction, citing Tafsīr ʿUthmānī:

1. **The Christians** who claimed that it was the Masīḥ (ʿalayhi al-salām) himself who asked them to believe in his sonship and godhead. On the logic above, this is exactly what a prophet can never have done.
2. **Muslims** who had gone to the Prophet ﷺ trying to find out whether it was all right for them to prostrate before him rather than greet him with the usual *salām* — and were chastised for it.
3. **The People of the Book** who had *"invested their rabbis and monks with the station of God."*

The lesson is one and the same in all three cases: reverence for a righteous man must never slide into worship of him.

## Ayah 83: the whole creation has already submitted

Ayah 83 turns to the audience with a question: *"Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?"* Ibn Kathir says Allah is rebuking those who prefer a religion other than the one He sent His Books and Messengers with — **the worship of Allah alone without partners**.

Then the ayah widens the frame: *to Him submitted all creatures in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.* Ibn Kathir brings other ayat alongside it — 13:15, that whoever is in the heavens and earth falls in prostration to Allah alone, willingly or unwillingly; and 16:48–50, where the shadows of created things incline to the right and to the left, making prostration unto Allah, lowly, and *"all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth, of the moving creatures and the angels"* prostrate and *are not proud*, fearing their Lord above them and doing what they are commanded.

Ibn Kathir then draws the distinction that gives the ayah its edge: **the faithful believer submits to Allah in heart and body, while the disbeliever unwillingly submits to Him in body only** — since he is under Allah's power, His irresistible control and mighty kingship, *"that cannot be repelled or resisted."* No one escapes submission. The only question is whether yours is willing.

Two early comments on *"willingly or unwillingly"* are preserved here, both reported by Wakīʿ. **Mujāhid** said the ayah is similar to 39:38 — *if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, surely they will say: Allah.* **Ibn ʿAbbās** said of the same phrase: *"When He took the covenant from them."*

The ayah closes: *"And to Him shall they all be returned"* — on the Day of Return, says Ibn Kathir, when He will reward or punish each person according to his or her deeds.

## Ayah 84: the confession a Muslim makes out loud

Ayah 84 is a command to declare: *Say: "We believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to us..."* Ibn Kathir walks through it phrase by phrase — *what has been sent down to us* is **the Qurʾān**; what was sent down to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb is **the scriptures and revelation**; **al-Asbāṭ** are *"the twelve tribes who originated from the twelve children of Israel (Yaʿqūb)"*; what was given to Mūsā and ʿĪsā is **the Tawrāh and the Injīl**; and *"the Prophets from their Lord"* — a phrase which, Ibn Kathir notes, **encompasses all of Allah's Prophets**.

Then the decisive clause: *"We make no distinction between one another among them"* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, **we believe in all of them**. And the seal: *"And to Him we have submitted."*

This is the practical shape of the covenant of ayah 81, now spoken by the community rather than the prophets. Ibn Kathir states it as a defining mark of the believers: *"faithful Muslims believe in every Prophet whom Allah has sent and in every Book He revealed, and never disbelieve in any of them."* Believing in some messengers while rejecting others is precisely what this confession rules out.

## Ayah 85: no religion but Islam

*"And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted of him."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact and worth memorising: **whoever seeks other than what Allah has legislated, it will not be accepted from him** — *"and in the Hereafter he will be one of the losers."*

He supports this with a saying of the Prophet ﷺ, which he introduces as an authentic hadith: **whoever commits an action that does not conform to our matter — our religion — then it is rejected.** (Ibn Kathir does not name a collection here, so it is left as he gives it.) The principle scales from the smallest act of worship to the choice of a religion itself: what Allah did not legislate, Allah does not accept.

**But what does "Islam" mean here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān devotes its commentary on this ayah to that question. Its literal meaning is **"submission and obedience."** As a term it stands for submission to that particular religion which Allah has sent through His prophets to guide human beings — *"because fundamental principles are the same in the religious codes of all prophets."* The Qurʾān uses the word in both senses: past prophets called themselves *Muslim* and their communities the *Muslim* community, and the name is also used as the particular name of the community of the Last of the Prophets ﷺ — as in *"It was He who named you Muslims before, and in this (Qurʾān)"* (22:78).

So which sense applies in ayah 85? Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's answer is that **whichever of the two meanings is taken, it does not make much difference in terms of the outcome**, and the reasoning is illuminating. The name "Islam" given to the religion of past prophets was for a limited group of people and a specified period of time; that code was not meant to serve as a universal code for all times to come. When a particular prophet departed and was replaced by another, the earlier code ceased to be operative, and the Islam of that time became what the new prophet presented. There was no difference between these codes in the fundamentals, though the subsidiary injunctions might differ. But **the Islam given through the last Prophet ﷺ is unabrogable and will serve as a permanent code right up to the Day of Judgment** — and by that same rule, all previous religions stand abrogated now that he ﷺ has been sent. *"Now, they are not Islam as such anymore. Instead, Islam is the name of that particular religion which has reached us through the Holy Prophet, Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān supports this with two reports it describes as appearing in authentic ahadith (it does not name a collection at this point, so they are left as it gives them): that the Prophet ﷺ said, **"Had Mūsā been living this day, following me would have been incumbent upon him too"**; and that **ʿĪsā (ʿalayhi al-salām), when he appears close to the Day of Resurrection, would — in spite of holding his distinction and office of prophethood — follow no other religious code except that of the Prophet ﷺ**.

See how neatly this closes the circle opened in ayah 81. Whichever sense of "Islam" you take, the outcome is the same: after the coming of the Last of the Prophets, only the religion that has come to the world through him will be termed Islam, and — in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's words — *"on belief in that alone depends the salvation نجات (najāt) of all human beings for it is their indispensable need."* (The tafsir notes that details on this subject have already appeared under 3:19.)

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, and no more than the sources support:

**Say the creed of ayah 84 and mean every name in it.** *We make no distinction between one another among them.* Ibn Kathir makes it a defining trait: believe in every Prophet Allah has sent and every Book He revealed, and never disbelieve in any of them.

**Let rank never become an excuse.** Even the prophets, having been given the knowledge and the prophethood, were not thereby excused from following and supporting the Prophet who comes after them — that is the plain force of ayat 81–82.

**Keep reverence and worship apart.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records the chastisement of Muslims who asked about prostrating to the Prophet ﷺ instead of greeting him with *salām*, and the admonishing of those who gave their rabbis and monks a station that belongs to Allah. Love your teachers; worship only Allah.

And underneath all of it, the sentence from ayah 83 that ought to stay with the reader: everything in the heavens and the earth is submitting to Allah already, willingly or unwillingly. The believer's submission is simply the willing kind — the heart joining what the body was never able to refuse.

passages.title: Disbelief after faith and the ransom refused
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat deal with the person who believed and then turned away from that belief — and with what awaits him if he never comes back. The passage moves in two waves: ayat 86–89 pronounce a severe sentence on the one who disbelieves after belief and then, at the very end, open a door for whoever repents; ayat 90–91 close that door on the one who dies still refusing, and picture him on the Day of Resurrection offering the whole earth in gold to buy his way out — and being turned down. Ibn Kathir's own heading over the first four is worth keeping in view: *Allah does not guide people who disbelieve after they believed, unless they repent.*

## The man who wanted to come back

Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas: a man from the Ansar embraced Islam, but later reverted and joined the polytheists. He later became sorry and sent his people with a message — *"Ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for me, if I can repent."* Then the ayat were revealed, from "How shall Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" through to "Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." His people sent word to him, and he re-embraced Islam.

Hold onto that. What was sent to that man was not the verdict alone, and not the pardon alone — it was this whole passage, the severity and the exception together, in one message. The severity is real. But the words were revealed for a man who was let back in.

Ibn Kathir notes that this wording is recorded by An-Nasa'i, Al-Hakim and Ibn Hibban, and that Al-Hakim said, "Its chain is Sahih and they did not record it."

## "How shall Allah guide...?" — ayah 86

The ayah lists exactly what makes their case so poor. They disbelieved **after their belief**. They **bore witness that the Messenger is true** — they testified to it themselves. And **clear proofs came to them**.

Ibn Kathir explains what that amounts to: the proofs and evidences were established, testifying to the truth of what the Messenger was sent with; the truth was thus explained to them, but they reverted to the darkness of polytheism. And so, in his striking phrase, "how can such people deserve guidance after they willingly leapt into utter blindness?"

Sit with the two images he uses, because they are his, not decoration added on top: light was given, and they went back into darkness; sight was available, and they leapt into blindness. The question is about *desert* — what is left to give a person who did that to himself?

This is why, Ibn Kathir says, Allah closed the ayah with **"And Allah guides not the people who are wrongdoers."**

## Does this mean an apostate can never be guided again?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises exactly the objection an honest reader will feel. On a superficial view of "How shall Allah give guidance..." (86), a doubt emerges that whoever turns apostate receives no guidance afterwards — although the fact is contrary to this. There are many who, after having become apostates, re-embrace the faith and become recipients of guidance.

The answer given (from *Bayān al-Qurʼān*) is that the withholding of guidance mentioned here is in accordance with **common usage** — ordinary human speech rather than a technical decree. The illustration offered: a criminal punished by a certain ruler might say, "I have been given a special treatment by the ruler with his own hands." And in answer it is said: "Why are we going to give a special treatment to such a criminal?" That is, there is just no special treatment called for in *this* case — it does not mean that such a person cannot, in any way, become deserving of it if he behaved well.

So ayah 86 speaks to what this conduct deserves; it is not a locked gate. That reading is borne out three ayat later by the exception in 89 — and borne out in history by the Ansari man himself, who came back.

## The sentence — ayat 87–88

Ayah 87 names their recompense: **"the curse of Allah, of the angels, and of all mankind."** Ibn Kathir's comment is compact and worth sitting with: *Allah curses them, and His creation also curses them.*

Then ayah 88: **"They will abide therein."** Therein *what*? Ibn Kathir is precise — *khālidīna fīhā*, "they will abide therein," means **in the curse**. The condemnation is not a moment; it is a permanent address.

**"Neither will their torment be lightened, nor will it be delayed or postponed."** Ibn Kathir: the torment will not be lessened, not even for an hour. Two mercies that human beings always hope for are named and withdrawn — a reduction in the sentence, and a stay of it. Neither is coming.

## The door — ayah 89

And then, immediately after that: **"Except for those who repent after that and do righteous deeds. Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."**

Notice that the ayah names two things and not one — they repent, *and* they do righteous deeds. Repentance here is not a private regret that leaves the life unchanged; it turns back and it then builds. The man of the Ansar did not merely feel sorry; he re-embraced Islam.

And notice how Allah closes the ayah — not with a further warning, but by describing Himself as Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful. Ibn Kathir's comment: this ayah indicates Allah's kindness, graciousness, compassion, mercy and favour on His creatures when they repent to Him, for He forgives them in this case. The severest passage in this stretch of the surah ends by advertising forgiveness.

## Ayah 90: when repentance is no longer accepted

Ayah 90 describes a different person: **"those who disbelieved after their belief and then went on increasing in their disbelief."** Not one lapse, but a trajectory. Of these it says: **"never will their repentance be accepted, and they are those who are astray."**

Ibn Kathir explains: Allah threatens and warns those who revert to disbelief after they believed and who thereafter **insist on disbelief until death** — in that case, no repentance shall be accepted from them upon their death. He supports this with Allah's words: *"And of no effect is the repentance of those who continue to do evil deeds until death faces one of them"* (4:18).

So the repentance the ayah refuses is the repentance offered at death itself, after a lifetime spent refusing. That is why 89 and 90 do not collide: 89 is repentance while the door is open; 90 is a hand reaching for the door after it has shut.

Of "and they are those who are astray," Ibn Kathir says the words go to those who abandon the path of truth for the path of wickedness.

Ibn Kathir also cites here a report from Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bazzar, from Ibn ʿAbbas: some people embraced Islam, reverted to disbelief, became Muslims again, then reverted from Islam. They sent their people inquiring about this matter, and they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — and this ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir comments that the chain of narration is satisfactory. The pattern in the report matches the words of the ayah exactly: not a single fall, but a habit of falling.

## Ayah 91: the ransom that buys nothing

Ayah 91 narrows to the final case: **"those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers."** Death has sealed it. And then the ayah measures what such a person could offer: **"the whole earth full of gold will not be accepted from anyone of them if they offered it as a ransom."**

Ibn Kathir draws the picture out — the earth's fill of gold: all of its mountains, hills, sand, dust, valleys, forests, land and sea. It still buys nothing.

He reads this in two directions, and both matter.

**First, gold spent in this life.** Those who die as disbelievers shall have no good deed ever accepted from them, even if they spent the earth's fill of gold in what was perceived to be an act of obedience. Ibn Kathir relates that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about ʿAbdullah bin Judʿan — who used to be generous to guests, helpful to the indebted, and who gave food to the poor — would all that benefit him? The Prophet ﷺ said: *"No, for not even one day during his life did he pronounce, 'O my Lord! Forgive my sins on the Day of Judgment.'"* (Ibn Kathir does not name a collection for this report here.) The point is not that generosity counts for nothing in itself; it is what the Prophet ﷺ put his finger on — the man never once, in an entire lifetime, turned to his Lord and asked.

**Second, gold offered on the Day itself.** Ibn Kathir lines up the parallels: *"nor shall compensation be accepted from him, nor shall intercession be of use to him"* (2:123); *"on which there will be neither mutual bargaining nor befriending"* (14:31); and *"Verily, those who disbelieve, if they had all that is in the earth, and as much again therewith to ransom themselves thereby from the torment on the Day of Resurrection, it would never be accepted of them, and theirs would be a painful torment"* (5:36). Payment, intercession, bargaining, friendship in high places — each is named and cancelled. The implication of the ayah, Ibn Kathir says, is that the disbeliever shall never avoid the torment of Allah.

### The two men brought forward

Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: a man from among the people of Paradise will be brought and Allah will ask him, "O son of Adam! How did you find your dwelling?" He will say, "O Lord, it is the best dwelling." Allah will say, "Ask and wish." The man will say, "I only ask and wish that You send me back to the world so that I am killed ten times in Your cause" — because of the honour of martyrdom he would experience. A man from among the people of the Fire will be brought, and Allah will say to him, "O son of Adam! How do you find your dwelling?" He will say, "It is the worst dwelling, O Lord." Allah will ask him, "Would you ransom yourself from Me with the earth's fill of gold?" He will say, "Yes, O Lord." Allah will say: **"You have lied. I asked you to do what is less and easier than that, but you did not do it"** — and he will be sent back to the Fire.

That last line is the heart of the passage. The ransom fails not only because the gold is worthless there, but because the offer is not believed: a man who would not do the lesser and easier thing when it was asked of him is not truly offering the whole earth now. And notice what the first man asks for — not more comfort, but the chance to give more.

The ayah closes: **"For them is a painful torment and they will have no helpers."** Ibn Kathir: they shall not have anyone who will save them from the torment of Allah or rescue them from His painful punishment. Wealth gone, intercession gone, allies gone.

## Living it

**Faith is not a possession; it is a state you must remain in.** The whole passage turns on the phrase "after their belief." Having once believed, once borne witness, once received the clear proofs, protects nobody by itself. Ayah 91 does not ask what a person believed at his best moment; it asks what he was when he died.

**What is asked of us is small — give it.** Ibn Judʿan fed the poor and helped the indebted, and was told it would not benefit him, because not one day of his life did he ask his Lord for forgiveness. And the man in the Fire is told that what was asked of him was *less and easier* than the earth's fill of gold. That is a mercy hidden inside a warning: the thing being asked is within reach right now.

**Never treat anyone's return as impossible.** These ayat contain some of the sternest language in the surah, and they were revealed in answer to a man asking whether he could still repent — and he came back to Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to shut down the misreading that an apostate can never be guided again; many, it says, re-embrace the faith and become recipients of guidance. If you know someone who has walked away, ayah 89 is still open: *repent, and do righteous deeds — Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.*

**And do not delay it.** That is the warning ayah 90 exists to give. Repentance is accepted — until it is insisted upon disbelief until death, and none of us knows when that hour arrives.

passages.title: Righteousness attained by giving what you love
passages.tafsir:
# Righteousness Attained by Giving What You Love (3:92)

This single ayah names the price of true righteousness: **you will not reach it until you spend out of what you love.** It closes with a reminder that nothing you give escapes Allah's knowledge — "and whatever of good you spend, Allah knows it well."

## Where this ayah sits

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the link with what came just before. In ayah 91 it was said that charity from those who disbelieve and deny is not acceptable with Allah. Now, in ayah 92, the address turns to the believers: they are told about acceptable charity and the etiquette that governs it.

## What does *birr* mean?

Everything in this ayah turns on one word: **بِرّ (birr)**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that its literal and real meaning is *the perfect fulfilment of someone's rights* — giving what is owed, fully and completely. It is also used in the sense of charity, the performance of good deeds, and beautiful conduct. A person who discharges every right due from him, fully and totally, is called **barr**. The Qur'an uses this very word of prophets who fulfilled their parents' rights perfectly: "good to my mother" (19:32) and "good to his father and mother" (19:14).

The plural of *barr* is **abrār**, "the righteous," a word the Qur'an repeats often:

- "Surely the righteous shall drink of a cup the mixture of which is camphor" (76:5)
- "Surely the righteous shall be in bliss, upon furnished thrones gazing" (83:22–23)

And its opposite is **fujūr** — sinfulness, disobedience — as we learn from "And surely, the sinners shall be in hell ablaze" (82:14).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith which sets *birr* and *fujūr* side by side. In **al-Adab al-Mufrad of Imam al-Bukhārī**, in **Ibn Mājah**, and in the **Musnad of Aḥmad**, it is reported from Sayyidunā Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Stick to speaking the truth, because truth is a companion of *birr*, and both these are in Paradise; and abstain from lying, because that is a companion of *fujūr*, and both these are in Hell."

So *birr* is not a vague warm feeling. It is a whole category of good with a destination attached. Ibn Kathir records that in his Tafsir, Wakīʿ reported that ʿAmr bin Maymūn said that "By no means shall you attain al-Birr" refers to **attaining Paradise**.

**And notice the scope of the word.** Surah al-Baqarah says: "Righteousness is not that you turn your faces to the East and the West; but righteousness is that one believes in Allah and the last Day…" (2:177). After giving a list of good deeds, that verse classes all of them as *birr*. Out of that wide range of righteous acts, our ayah singles out **one** as the most preferred form: to spend the most cherished things in the way of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: entering the ranks of the *abrār* depends on sacrificing, for Allah's sake, that which you hold dear.

## How the Companions heard it

The most illuminating thing about this ayah is what happened the moment it was revealed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it: the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), who were the first addressees of the Qur'anic injunctions and the direct disciples of the Prophet ﷺ, really loved to carry out those injunctions in letter and spirit. When this ayah came down, **each one of them surveyed what he owned to find what he loved most** — and requests began arriving before the Prophet ﷺ that these very things be spent in the way of Allah.

### Abū Ṭalḥah and the garden of Bayruḥāʾ

Ibn Kathir reports that **Imam Aḥmad** recorded from Anas bin Mālik: Abū Ṭalḥah had more property than any other of the Anṣār in Madinah, and the most beloved of his property to him was the garden of Bayruḥāʾ, which lay in front of the Prophet's Masjid. The Prophet ﷺ used to go into the garden and drink its fresh water. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the garden had a well called Biʾr Ḥāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ liked its water, and that the farm was very precious, fertile, and the dearest of all Abū Ṭalḥah owned.

When this ayah was revealed, Abū Ṭalḥah came and said: "O Messenger of Allah! Allah says, *By no means shall you attain al-Birr unless you spend of that which you love.* No doubt, Bayruḥāʾ is the most beloved of all my property to me. So I want to give it in charity in Allah's cause, and I expect its reward and compensation from Allah. O Messenger of Allah, spend it where Allah makes you think is feasible."

The Prophet ﷺ replied: **"Well done! It is profitable property, it is profitable property. I have heard what you have said, and I think it would be proper if you gave it to your kith and kin."**

Abū Ṭalḥah said, "I will do so, O Messenger of Allah," and distributed the garden among his relatives and cousins. Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was recorded in the **Two Ṣaḥīḥs**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise cites **al-Bukhārī and Muslim**.
