- "On the day of Doom, you shall see those who lied against Allah (with) their faces blackened" (39:60);
- "Some faces on that day shall shine, laughing, joyous. Some faces on that day shall be dusty, overspread with darkness" (80:38–41) — where the words *ghabarah* (dust) and *qatarah* (an overspreading gloom) carry the sense;
- "Faces on that day shall be radiant, looking towards their Lord" (75:22) — *nāḍirah*, radiance.

The words *bayāḍ* (whiteness) and *sawād* (blackness) in our ayah, it notes, belong to that same family of expressions.

According to the majority of commentators, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the brightness is **the brightness of the light of faith**: the faces of the believers will be resplendent with that light, fresh and smiling from the happiness of the rewards Allah has bestowed on them. The darkness is **the darkness of disbelief**: the faces of the disbelievers covered with the gloomy anguish of disbelief, with "the added soot of sin and transgression" turning them still darker.

## Who are these people?

The early commentators identified the two groups in several ways, and the sources preserve the difference of view rather than flattening it.

**Ibn 'Abbas** (radiy Allahu 'anhu), as cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the faces of the followers of the Sunnah — the Prophet's ﷺ way — will be bright, and the faces of the followers of *bid'ah* — innovation in the revealed faith, something neither Allah nor His Messenger ﷺ intended — will be dark. Ibn Kathir reports the same view from Ibn 'Abbas, phrasing it as the faces of the followers of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah (the united main body of the Muslims) radiating with whiteness, and the faces of the followers of innovation and division being darkened.

**'Ata'** (rahimahullah), as cited from Qurtubi: the bright faces are those of the Muhajirin and the Ansar; the dark faces those of Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir.

**'Ikrimah** (radiy Allahu 'anhu), also from Qurtubi: the dark faces belong to those of the People of the Book who had confirmed the coming of the Prophet ﷺ before he was ordained, but who — once he had been given prophethood — did not accept or support him, and instead set about falsifying him.

**Al-Hasan Al-Basri**, quoted by Ibn Kathir on the words "Did you reject faith after accepting it?": "They are the hypocrites."

**From the Sunnah:** Abu 'Isa At-Tirmidhi recorded that Abu Ghalib said that Abu Umamah saw heads of the Khawarij hanging on the streets of Damascus and commented, "The Dogs of the Fire and the worst dead people under the cover of the sky. The best dead men are those whom these have killed" — then recited "On the Day when some faces will become white and some faces will become black" to the end of the ayah. Asked whether he had heard this from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he replied, "If I only heard it from the Messenger of Allah once, twice, thrice, four times, or seven times, I would not have narrated it to you." At-Tirmidhi said, "This Hadith is Hasan." Ibn Majah and Ahmad recorded similarly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same report from Tirmidhi, applying the dark faces to the Khawarij and the bright faces to those whom they killed.

**How to hold these together.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that there are further explanations besides these, but that they all lead to the same conclusion and are not contradictory — each names a striking instance of one underlying reality. Imam al-Qurtubi's own summary gathers them: the faces of sincere Muslims will be bright, while the faces of all those who altered their religion, or became apostates and disbelievers, or concealed hypocrisy in their hearts, will be dark. Ibn Kathir reaches the same breadth from the other end: after "Then taste the torment for rejecting faith," he comments simply that "this description befits every disbeliever."

## "Did you reject faith after accepting it?"

The words spoken to the darkened faces in ayah 106 come as a question: *akafartum ba'da imanikum*, "Did you reject faith after accepting it?" It is worth noticing that all three of the identifications the commentators give sit naturally under a question of that shape — Al-Hasan Al-Basri's hypocrites, 'Ikrimah's People of the Book who had confirmed the Prophet ﷺ and then turned against him, and Qurtubi's summary naming those who altered their religion or became apostates.

Then: "So taste the torment for rejecting faith."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this closing phrase — "now taste the punishment because you have been sinning" — indicates: the punishment of that Day is not an arbitrary imposition, but the consequence of what a person earned while living his mortal life. In its striking phrase, the blessings of Paradise and the hardships of Hell "are simply a changed form of our very deeds."

## Mercy is what the passage is built around

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine observation about the ordering of the two groups. In the opening statement of ayah 106, brightness is mentioned first and darkness after it. But when the detail begins — "As for those whose faces turn dark" — darkness is placed before brightness, although the sequence of the original statement would have required brightness first here as well.

This reversal, it suggests, points to Allah's main purpose in creating: **to bless His creation with His mercy; punishment is not the objective.** Those with bright faces come first, as the ones who deserve mercy and merit from their Lord. Then, at the close of the passage in ayah 107, "they will be in Allah's mercy, therein they shall dwell forever" — and named there, it says, very affectionately. So those deserving of mercy are identified at the very beginning and again at the end, and the mention of those whose faces turn dark remains *in between*. All of this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, points to Allah's limitless, endless mercy: human beings were certainly not created to serve as an exhibit of divine punishment, but to flourish under the sunshine of Allah's mercy.

**Why "Allah's mercy" rather than "Paradise"?** Ayah 107 does not say "they will be in the Garden"; it says "they will be in Allah's mercy." Ibn 'Abbas explained that *rahmah*, mercy, means Jannah — Paradise — here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Tafsir al-Kabir, draws out the wisdom in the choice of word: no one, however worshipful and pious, enters Paradise except through the sole mercy of Allah. Being devoted in acts of worship is not a feat of human excellence as such — the very ability to worship is itself a gift of Allah. Worship does not in itself create an inherent right to enter Paradise; it is Allah's mercy alone through which one enjoys its bliss.

**And it does not run out.** "They will be in Allah's mercy" is immediately qualified by *hum fīhā khālidūn*, "therein they shall dwell forever." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this means the mercy the believers rest in will not be temporary: it will be forever and eternal, never taken away and never reduced in their case. By contrast, it observes, in the case of those whose faces turn dark, it is not expressly mentioned here whether they will remain in that state forever. Ibn Kathir adds the same note of settled permanence about the believers: they will reside in Paradise for eternity, and shall never desire to be removed.

## Ayah 108: recited in truth, and no injustice

"These are the Ayat of Allah. We recite them to you" — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, these are the verses of Allah, His proofs and signs that He reveals to you, O Muhammad ﷺ. And *bil-ḥaqq*, "in truth": making known the true reality of this world and the Hereafter.

"And Allah wills no injustice to the 'Alamin" — the '*Alamin* meaning all the worlds, everyone in them. Ibn Kathir: He never treats them with injustice; rather, He is the Just Ruler who is able to do everything and has knowledge of everything, and therefore He has no need to treat any of His creatures with injustice. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties the same words back to the earning of punishment in ayah 106: whatever reward or punishment there is, is nothing but justice, and very much the perfect expression of divine wisdom and mercy.

## Ayah 109: everything belongs to Him, everything returns to Him

"And to Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth" — they are all, Ibn Kathir says, His servants and His property. "And all matters go back to Allah" — for His is the decision concerning the affairs of this life and the Hereafter, and His is the supreme authority in both.

Notice how this closes the passage. Ibn Kathir presents ayah 109 as following directly from the statement before it: it is *because* He is the Just Ruler with power and knowledge over everything, "and this is why He said next" that everything in the heavens and the earth is His and every matter returns to Him. The final ayah is not a change of subject; it is bound to the assurance that the judgement of ayat 106–107 carries no injustice at all.

## Living it

**Hold to the Sunnah and to the united body of the Muslims.** Ibn 'Abbas's reading of the two colours — brightness for the followers of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, darkness for the followers of innovation and division — and Ibn Kathir's own heading over this passage, on unity and the consequence of division, both put the matter in the same place: how you stood towards the community of the Prophet's ﷺ way is not a question of temperament. It is something the sources say will one day show on the face.

**Let the fear be of turning back, not merely of falling short.** The question in ayah 106 is put to people who had faith, or who had confirmed the truth and then refused it. Ask Allah to keep you from being among them.

**And let hope have the last word.** The shape of this passage — mercy named at its opening, mercy named again at its close, and the warning held in between — is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it, deliberate. You were not created to be an exhibit of divine punishment. You were created to flourish under the sunshine of Allah's mercy — and even then, not by the weight of your worship, but by that mercy alone.
